The new label is based on sanitary measures to support the return to business in the hospitality and restaurant industry

Accor and Bureau Veritas, a world-leading provider in testing, inspection and certification, launched a label designed to certify that the appropriate safety standards and cleaning protocols have been achieved to allow businesses to reopen.

The label will cover both accommodation and catering, and will set the sanitary standards applicable to all the Group’s hotels as well as to other chains and independent hotels. The project was carried out in partnership with doctors and epidemiologists, and has been developed in collaboration with Accor owners and trade associations, such as UMIH, GNC, and GNI.

The project will be shared next week within Alliance France Tourisme as well as with the relevant ministries (French Ministries of Tourism, Health and Labor) so that they are actively involved in – and validate – the recommended standards. Concrete proposals will be submitted, in France and subsequently in Europe, to the various governments, relevant ministries and committees for the easing of lockdown measures. Concretely, the output of this effort will be an operational guide made available to all stakeholders in the hospitality industry, enabling them to rigorously apply the health and safety recommendation of authories (WHO, Health Ministry etc), both in guest services spaces and in back office and catering spaces. European customers will be able to check on a dedicated Bureau Veritas website, before they book their next stay whether any hotel or restaurant has been certified or not by Bureau Veritas.

Franck GERVAIS, CEO Europe Accor, said, "Welcoming, protecting and taking care of others is the very DNA of Accor and at the heart of what we do. Today, more than ever, our employees, customers and partners need to be reassured of our ability to offering them the best welcome possible. As the European leader in hospitality, it is our duty to anticipate needs and respond to health and safety requirements by adhering to the highest standards. We are pleased to be pioneering this drive with Bureau Veritas and to extend it to all stakeholders.”

USIDE’s work is based on recognized scientific methodologies, which the firm has developed in accordance with French and international standards. With a team of 70 consultants, led by Eric Albert (Managing Partner and psychiatrist), Laurence Saunder (Managing Partner), and Jean-Luc Emery (Partner and psychiatrist), USIDE generates approximately 10 million euros in annual revenue.

# Agility: why having this capability in your organization is so critical

The final HR committee of 2019 was focused on the much talked about topic of organizational agility, the new strategic imperative of the 21 st century. Over 20 participants from a wide range of industries and functions came to listen to Ron Stewart, President of Prosci Canada, who divided his presentation in three main parts: “Making a compelling case for agility”, “What are the attributes of agile organization” and “How change management enables agility”.

After a definition of the meaning of agility in a business context, Ron introduced us to the ADKAR model which outlines the 5 steps to follow to be prepared for an organizational change: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability and Reinforcement. He then explained how to go from the big picture of the change you wish to implement to the detailed actions you need to put in place throughout the organization to make the change successful. Through a series of examples, Ron showed us that any kind of change can impact your employees’ mindset and give an unexpected turn of events to the vision of your initial project, if not anticipated and communicated properly. In one word: be prepared!

# Air France chooses Michelin as its exclusive tyre supplier as part of an ambitious ten-year partnership

Air France has renewed its trust in Michelin and has selected the French group as the exclusive tyre supplier for its aircraft fleet. The Michelin Group will equip the company's short-, medium- and long-haul aircraft1 with new or retreaded tyres notably produced at the Saint Doulchard plant in Bourges, France.

Air France's aircraft will be equipped with the most modern aircraft tyres, such as Radial Michelin® AIR X tyres incorporating NZG (Near Zero Growth) technology. Designed to guarantee a constant tyre diametre, this technology provides aircraft tyres with greater durability and exceptional resistance.

Pioneers in the field of French aviation and historic partners, Air France and Michelin have always shared a common DNA: innovation at the service of performance and safety.

Between 2010 and 2020, the partnership has enabled Air France to benefit from all the latest technologies developed by Michelin. Over the next ten years, both groups will continue to work together and steer the field of innovation towards a shared ambition, to reduce the carbon footprint. Michelin takes an active part in European research programmes and is working on breakthrough technologies to continue to lighten its tyres and associated systems and to mechanically reduce fuel consumption and CO2 emissions on each flight.

Air France and Michelin will also extend their partnership to digital and other services. Michelin will offer Air France even more ambitious solutions such as its innovative recycling channels, its highperformance ecological resins and its 3D metal and plastic printing expertise. With "Ready to Fly", the airline goes one step further by offering its customers the certainty of knowing that they have all the health documents required for their trip before they arrive at the airport. A few days before departure, customers travelling on eligible flights receive an email inviting them to upload their health documents on an Air France online platform. These documents are then checked and if they are complete and correct, a confirmation message is sent to the customer. # Air France: their new commitment to health and safety to ensure you a safe trip

Find out, in video, the Air France's new commitment to health and safety

The health and well-being of customers and staff are at the heart of Air France’s concerns. In addition to the strict hygiene procedures routinely applied to its flights, Air France has decided to reinforce its health measures for everyone’s protection at the airport and on board its aircraft. These hygiene measures are implemented throughout the customer journey.

- The wearing of masks will be compulsory on our flights as from 11 May 2020. All customers will have to wear a mask throughout their journey. Customers will be notified of this via all communication channels (email, sms, websites) prior to their departure and will be asked to ensure they possess one or more masks for their trip.

- At the airport, the measures implemented guarantee a travel experience in optimum conditions of health and safety, with the application of physical distancing measures, counters equipped with Plexiglass protection screens, regularly disinfected self-service kiosks, hand sanitizer available throughout the airport and the reorganization of customer channels at check-in and boarding to limit contact

- On board the majority of flights, the current low load factors allow us to respect physical distancing. In cases where this is not possible, requiring all passengers and crew members to wear masks ensures adequate health protection.

- Air France has reinforced aircraft cleaning procedures, notably with the disinfection of all surfaces in contact with customers such as armrests, tables and screens, and the introduction of a specific procedure for disinfecting aircraft by spraying an approved virucidal product.

- The air in the cabin is renewed every 3 minutes. The air recycling system on board Air France aircraft is equipped with HEPA – High Efficiency Particulate Air – filters identical to those used in hospital operating theatres.

- To limit interaction, the in-flight service has been simplified – the meal and beverage service has been completed adapted, and duty-free sales and the newspapers and magazines offer have been temporarily suspended.

# Air Liquide collaborates with Itochu to scale up Japan hydrogen mobility markets

Air Liquide Japan and Itochu Corporation (Itochu) have signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on the development of hydrogen mobility markets in Japan.

Air Liquide Japan and Itochu will initially focus on the development of the hydrogen retail infrastructure in Japan, both for passenger vehicles and for the new fleets of commercial vehicles (trucks, busses). The objective is to expand this retail infrastructure and develop a competitive hydrogen supply offer for passenger and commercial end-users, in collaboration with public authorities, allowing a rapid ramp-up of hydrogen mobility in Japan. The two companies will investigate more globally the opportunities to scale up the hydrogen supply chain in support of the Japan Government hydrogen roadmap.

This collaboration will leverage the expertise and technologies of Air Liquide across the hydrogen supply chain and the large footprint of Itochu Group across multiple energy sectors , from fuel retail business to renewable energy production plants.

This collaboration comes after the recent announcement by the Japanese Government of the Green Society plan , to reach carbon neutrality by 2050, in which hydrogen is anticipated to take a key role. Under this plan, the Japanese government will ban the sales of vehicles which completely run on fossil fuels after 2035, pushing for the transportation sector to make a shift toward battery electric and fuel cell electric vehicles.

François Abrial, Member of the Air Liquide Group’s Executive Committee supervising Asia Pacific, said:

“The fight against climate change is at the heart of Air Liquide 's strategy. Hydrogen is projected to play a key role in supporting energy transition and the emergence of a carbon-neutral society. With this collaboration, we seek to jointly accelerate the development of Hydrogen mobility markets in Japan, leveraging our complementary technology portfolios and know-how across the entire hydrogen value chain. ”

# April: what's changing in Japan

Food prices, home delivery services, car-sharing... Everything that is changing in Japan from April.

- ​​​​​​ End of carpooling ban

The ban on carpooling will be lifted in certain areas (Tokyo, Kanagawa, Aichi, Kyoto) under certain conditions (days and times). Fares will still remain the same as for cabs.

Non-governmental organizations will be the main operators in areas where there is a shortage of cabs and other means of transport, with fares varying according to supply and demand.

- Rising food prices

Food prices are set to continue rising in April. According to data from Teikoku Databank, traditionally high prices for raw materials and energy, combined with rising logistics and labor costs, are expected to result in a rapid rise of over 3,000 items in April (mainly processed food products).

- Coronavirus vaccines to be paid for under certain conditions

The reimbursement of drugs and vaccines against the new coronavirus will be reviewed. For example, the Zocova coronavirus vaccine is expected to cost more than 15,000 yen for those benefiting from a 70% health insurance discount.

People over 65 will benefit from a “co-payment” of up to 7,000 yen, allowing them to be vaccinated once a year from autumn to winter.

Treatment for people under 65 will be considered as “voluntary vaccinations”, and the full amount will have to be paid by each individual in principle.

- Capping of overtime

Following the labor reform law passed in 2018, overtime will be capped in certain sector. These include doctors (960 hours a year - with the exception of doctors and trainees in charge of emergencies and in rural areas), drivers in the transport sector (960 hours a year) as well as construction workers (360 hours a year).

- Higher prices for medical consultations

In this new episode of Business - France-Japan Cross Perspectives , we meet Julien Major, Managing Director of Groupe SEB Japan Co., Ltd., on the occasion of Tefal's 70th anniversary. Drawing on his international experience, particularly in Japan, he highlights several fundamental values that shape Franco-Japanese business relations, including humility, collaborative work, and the search for consensus. In Japan, major decisions are carefully prepared through a consensus-building process known as nemawashi before being formally approved and publicly announced.

"There is great importance placed on aligning stakeholders before making a decision public."

Japan: A Market Where Quality Allows No Compromise

According to Julien Major, the greatest challenge of the Japanese market lies in its exceptionally high quality standards. Japanese consumers evaluate not only the product itself but every aspect of the customer experience, including the packaging. This pursuit of "zero defects" encourages Groupe SEB Japan Co., Ltd.to systematically adapt its products to local habits rather than simply exporting models designed for other markets. This requires close collaboration between the Japanese teams and the group's international R&D centers to develop products specifically tailored to the expectations of Japanese consumers.

Innovation as the Key to Success

# Business Regards croisés - 70 Years of Tefal, 50 Years in Japan

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/business-regards-croises-70-years-of-tefal-50-years-in-japan.html
Innovation as the Key to Success

Tefal's strong position in Japan is built above all on innovation. In the early 2000s, Tefal brand Japan introduced electric kettles to a market where water was still predominantly heated on gas stoves. By emphasizing speed, safety, and energy efficiency, the company gradually transformed consumer habits. Today, innovation remains at the heart of the group's strategy. As Japanese homes tend to be more compact than their European counterparts, consumers favor versatile, space-saving, and easy-to-use appliances. This philosophy also led Groupe to enter one of Japan's most symbolic product categories: rice cookers, using infrared cooking technology developed by one of its Chinese subsidiaries.

Decide Slowly, Execute Quickly

Beyond product development, Julien Major also spoke about Japan's management culture. Compared with Europe, decision-making in Japan tends to devote more time to consultation and consensus-building among stakeholders. However, once a direction has been agreed upon, the entire organization shares a common understanding, allowing decisions to be executed quickly and in a coordinated manner. Managers assigned from overseas are expected to be good listeners and willing to reassess their own ways of working. Julien Major believes that, as an expatriate, it is first and foremost the manager's responsibility to adapt to the local environment, rather than expecting the environment to adapt to them.

Made in France, Adapted for Japan

Contrary to common assumptions, a large share of the products sold in Japan continues to be manufactured in France, particularly in Groupe SEB's factories in the Savoie region. This French manufacturing heritage reflects the group's industrial expertise, even though many Japanese consumers are unaware of the brand's French origins. In fact, some even perceive Tefal as a Japanese brand, illustrating just how successfully it has become embedded in the Japanese market.

In a mature market, Groupe SEB Japan Co., Ltd.continues to rely on innovation by creating entirely new product categories rather than simply following existing trends. According to Julien Major, companies willing to take risks and introduce genuine innovations will continue to stand out, even in a market often regarded as conservative.

During this episode, Christophe Avenel looks back on the history of AXA’s establishment in Japan and on the integration of Nippon Dantai in the early 2000s, considered a decisive step in the Group’s development among Japanese SMEs.

This long-standing presence also allows AXA to closely observe the evolution of the Japanese economy and the changes affecting companies and households.

From savings to investment

After several decades of deflation and rates close to zero, Japan is entering a new period: inflation, rising interest rates and the development of NISA could gradually change the savings habits of Japanese households, a significant part of whose savings is still held in cash or deposits.

For AXA, this evolution opens up new perspectives, particularly around products combining savings and protection. But it also raises a broader question: how will Japanese people change their relationship with investment after decades of low inflation and very low interest rates?

A new transformation with artificial intelligence

Like the financial sector as a whole, insurance is also facing the rise of artificial intelligence. For AXA Japan, the applications are numerous: customer relations, automation, software development or even employee productivity.

# Business regards croisés - Danone: The HR challenges of foreign companies in Japan

In this new episode of Business – Cross Perspectives , we meet Jean-Renaud Humblot, who joined Danone as HR Director for Japan and South Korea after six years in Australia and New Zealand. Leading human resources in a highly competitive environment, he shares insights into the challenges faced by foreign companies in Japan and the country’s strategic importance for the group.

“Japan is a Danone superstar”

Attracting talent in an ultra-competitive gaishikei market

For gaishikei —foreign companies established in Japan—the job market and talent management are extremely competitive. Indeed, looking for profiles that combine strong expertise with a good command of English immediately limits the pool of candidates. Talent with experience in multinational corporations (MNCs) represents only about 2% of Japan’s workforce. As a result, competition between companies for these profiles is particularly intense.

The loyalty of Japanese employees is often described as legendary. Even in a foreign company like Danone, some employees can reach 15, 20 or even 35 years of tenure. However, in the gaishikei environment, talents tend to have greater mobility as they can leverage competition between companies. Despite this, genuine loyalty remains, especially when employees identify with the company’s culture and values.

Reading between the lines: the intercultural challenge

When faced with communication gaps between French and Japanese professionals, one quickly notices that interactions in Japan tend to be less direct. It is therefore necessary to learn how to read between the lines and understand non-verbal signals. This cultural subtlety can sometimes be surprising.

Jean-Renaud Humblot notably mentions his discovery of taishoku daikō , agencies that handle employee resignations on their behalf.

When such situations occur, questions arise: at what point did dialogue break down? Why did the employee not feel comfortable enough to express their difficulties or discuss resignation internally? For HR teams, this highlights the importance of creating an environment built on trust and open communication.

# Business Regards croisés – MCDecaux is revolutionizing urban advertising in Japan

In this new episode of Business Cross Perspectives, we meet Malik Roumane, President & CEO of JCDecaux Japan (MCDecaux). Drawing on a rich career spanning industry, luxury, and B2B, he shares his vision of a unique model that combines innovation, public service, and local adaptation in Japan’s demanding market.

"Everyone has to benefit from it: the city, the user, and the advertiser."

Malik Roumane’s career path

Malik Roumane’s journey in Japan follows a three-stage trajectory. He began in industry, notably with Saint-Gobain, working between France and Japan, where he developed strong expertise in structured and technical environments. He then spent around ten years in the luxury sector with Richemont before transitioning into B2B.

This third chapter led him to manage various business activities in Japan, culminating in his appointment as head of JCDecaux three and a half years ago. This diversity of experience is now a key asset in the way he leads the company, combining operational excellence, brand sensitivity, and a deep understanding of local dynamics.

JCDecaux: a unique model serving cities

Founded in 1964, JCDecaux is built on a simple yet revolutionary idea: financing street furniture through advertising. This model enables cities to benefit from modern, well-maintained, and evolving infrastructure without direct cost to public finances.

Beyond bus shelters, the offering has significantly expanded over time to include digital services, connectivity, charging solutions, and even initiatives contributing to urban greening. The challenge is no longer just to install infrastructure, but to meet the evolving needs of cities and their residents with a long-term perspective.

A pioneering presence in Japan

JCDecaux’s entry into Japan is a textbook case. At the time, advertising in public spaces was not permitted, making the model initially inapplicable. It required extensive engagement with authorities, particularly the MLIT, to demonstrate its benefits.

Innovation and Digital

Technological advancements are opening up new opportunities for the industry. The growth of digital media enables far more agile and targeted delivery of advertising campaigns. Through programmatic buying, advertisers can tailor their messages based on time, location, or external factors such as weather conditions.

This flexibility creates new ways to engage audiences, while maintaining strong complementarity with traditional formats, which ensure continuous presence and high visibility.

In Japan, street furniture also plays a vital role in public communication, particularly in the event of natural disasters. Digital displays can be immediately activated by authorities to broadcast alerts, guide the public, and support crisis management. This function further strengthens JCDecaux’s position as an integrated urban player, beyond its advertising role.

Supporting Japan’s Internationalization

In a context of demographic decline, Japan is increasingly required to evolve by integrating more international talent. For Malik Roumane, this transformation is both inevitable and an opportunity.

The goal is to build an environment capable of balancing Japan’s unique characteristics with growing global openness. In the long term, business success will depend on the ability to create hybrid organizations that combine cultures and expertise, while maintaining the right balance within the local context.

The company can manage events of widely varying sizes, including operations for up to 2,500 people. It also adapts to tight deadlines, extended hours, and complex requirements. Its operations rely on a dedicated kitchen, in-house logistics with its own refrigerated vehicles, and equipment capable of handling large volumes and multiple events simultaneously. This operational control strengthens its ability to deliver reliable, high-quality services under any constraints.

Expertise in Under-Served Specific Needs

Certain segments of the Japanese catering market remain underdeveloped, particularly when it comes to specific dietary requirements. Tokyo Catering Club has positioned itself to meet needs such as halal-friendly, vegan, and gluten-free options, while also incorporating diverse cultural expectations. This expertise allows the company to work with embassies, Middle Eastern clients, and foreign cultural institutions organizing events in Tokyo. # CCI France Japon and CNCPI sign a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen cooperation in economics, innovation, and intellectual property between Japan and France

During a joint event held in Tokyo on Wednesday, June 4, 2025, in the presence of Nicolas Bonnardel, Managing Director of CCI France Japon, and Emmanuel Potdevin, President of the CNCPI, the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCI France Japon) and the CNCPI (National Council of Industrial Property Attorneys) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to strengthen and promote economic and trade relations between Japanese and French businesses, focusing on the following key areas:

- Sharing of information, knowledge, and best practices in the fields of intellectual property, innovation, and creativity for the benefit of companies and project leaders

- Facilitating connections and mentorship between members of both organizations

- Promoting business partnerships between French and Japanese companies

- Co-organizing joint events (study tours, workshops, seminars, webinars, and B2B missions)

About CCI France Japon:

The French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCI France Japon) is the leading European Chamber in Japan. Founded in 1918, it brings together a network of over 700 member companies across all sectors, including one-third Japanese firms. CCI France Japon is a member of CCI France International (120 chambers in 95 countries, representing 36,000 companies worldwide) and the European Business Council – European Chamber (22 industry committees).

About CNCPI: The CNCPI , Compagnie Nationale des Conseils en Propriété Industrielle , represents 1,130 Industrial Property Attorneys practicing in France. Their core mission is to support companies in the protection, defense, and enhancement of their intellectual property rights (trademarks, patents, designs, software, personal data, digital law, etc.). The CNCPI advocates for a bold innovation policy backed by intellectual property—an essential tool for innovation—working in close collaboration with political and economic decision-makers and relevant industry networks.

The French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan announced that it will open a branch office in Fukui.

# CCIFJ and the Japan Institute for Overseas Investment strengthen their cooperation

The French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCIFJ) and the Japan Institute for Overseas Investment (JOI) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on October 6, 2026, aimed at strengthening their cooperation and fostering investment and economic ties between France and Japan.

The agreement was signed by Jérôme Chouchan, President of CCIFJ, and Kenichiro Hayashi, President of the Japan Institute for Overseas Investment.

Established to contribute to the development of economic relations between Japan and other countries, JOI supports Japanese companies in their international investments, notably through research, analysis and the dissemination of information. For its part, CCIFJ helps Japanese companies and investors better understand the French market, its investment opportunities and its economic environment. The new agreement formalizes the two organizations’ commitment to working more closely together to promote Japanese direct investment in France.

### A Practical Partnership Serving Businesses

The cooperation will include regular exchanges of information on France’s investment environment and conditions, as well as on opportunities for cooperation between French and Japanese companies. The two organizations will also be able to share and promote their respective activities and facilitate networking opportunities between their business communities.

The partnership also provides for cooperation in organizing seminars and roundtable discussions designed to provide companies with better information on economic and investment opportunities. JOI may also promote selected information and initiatives from CCIFJ on its website.

Finally, CCIFJ will be able to support JOI’s research activities related to Japanese direct investment in France, notably by providing relevant information and facilitating introductions to key stakeholders.

### Building Stronger Bridges Between the French and Japanese Business Ecosystems

Through this MOU, CCIFJ is strengthening its role as a bridge between the French and Japanese business communities. The objective is to facilitate Japanese companies’ access to information about the French market while creating more opportunities for meetings, dialogue and cooperation between businesses from both countries.

This partnership with JOI will therefore create new channels for exchange and help raise awareness among Japanese companies of the opportunities France has to offer.

From February 26 to 28, 2026, the city of Ogaki hosted for the first time a major gastronomic and cultural event with a cheese competition organized by the MOF Museum Nagoya , supported by the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCIFJ) and the City of Ogaki. At the heart of the three-day program was a cheese competition inviting participants to create artistic and culinary works highlighting cheese in innovative ways. Contestants designed original constructions including sculptures and cheese pyramids showcasing both creativity and technical skill.

A distinctive feature of this edition was the use of both French and Japanese cheeses, illustrating the growing dialogue between the cheesemaking traditions of the two countries as well as the rising quality of Japanese local production. The creations were evaluated by a jury based on two complementary criteria: visual aesthetics and taste quality, emphasizing the balance between artistic expression and gastronomic excellence.

## Exceptional Demonstrations by Meilleurs Ouvriers de France

Among the highlights of the event were live demonstrations conducted by Meilleurs Ouvriers de France who traveled from France, including Dominique Bouchait , Meilleur Ouvrier de France cheesemonger and Christian Vabret , Meilleur Ouvrier de France baker. In front of an engaged audience, the artisans created impressive Eiffel Towers made entirely of cheese, demonstrating the precision, creativity, and expertise associated with the prestigious MOF title.

# An Overview of Factory Automation in Japan by Stäubli

For the 6th edition of our Kansai Sectoral Gatherings, we visited Stäubli's showroom in Umeda, talking Factory Automation among a throng of robots.

Yesterday, we held our sixth edition of this year’s sectoral gatherings at Stäubli ’s showroom, right next to Umeda. Stäubli’s team had prepared a stunning presentation that was giving a broad overview of the situation of Factory Automation in Japan.

Stäubli is a Switzerland-based company that has 130 years of experience in automation, starting with weaving machines and working its way through specialized connectors and robots, thanks to a mix of innovation and acquisition . They now have expertise in 20 different industrial segments , which gives them a diverse vision of the issues arising in the industry.

# An Overview of Factory Automation in Japan by Stäubli

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/conference-report-the-state-of-factory-automation-in-japan-by-staeubli-in-osaka.html
The assessment regarding Japan is actually quite gloomy , and we could only make rather negative observations: despite a rapidly aging population that would require the society to replace the decreasing workforce with automated solutions whenever it can, automation in Japan is actually lagging behind and moving at a slow pace. We drew the same conclusions earlier this year regarding the related subject of digital transformation . As a result, Japan’s productivity is taking a worrying dip , with people working long hours to produce less than other countries with better work-life balance. At the same time, Japan’s industry is lacking the innovation necessary to compete internationally. It was observed that the comfort offered by Japanese society tends to make people afraid to take risks and try new solutions. As a consequence, Japan often waits for others to develop and try new solutions before adopting them, which means that the Japanese industry does not offer solutions that would stand out on the market. Despite the current depreciation of the yen and Japan's manufacturing capacity, we can only notice that exports are low . Finally, you would think that introducing robots in the production lines would be perceived as labor cost reduction, but high-end robots and their inclusion itself are actually very expensive and require a lot of investments that many companies are not willing to make. Then, introducing robots in a production line also means more qualified employees , because it takes much more skills and knowledge to program, repair or maintain a robot than to just perform the task taken up by it.

As Stäubli’s speakers pointed out however, factory automation could bring many positive improvements to Japan’s economy. First of all, robots can perform better, more precise tasks than humans , and with a much lower rate of mistakes . As such, introducing more robots could allow Japan to shine once more in the field of very high-end technological products, singling itself out from its local competitors in the manufacturing industry. Obviously, automation would also be an answer to the aging population and the dire necessity to increase production drastically to keep up the pace and provide enough revenue for the elderly.

# An Overview of Factory Automation in Japan by Stäubli

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/conference-report-the-state-of-factory-automation-in-japan-by-staeubli-in-osaka.html
The bottom line of this overview was that Japan in general and Kansai in particular are a manufacturing country/region. It has the potential to become a truly productive place for high-end products and take the lead again in specific fields. However, it needs to face and address its issues without any delay if it does not want to fall behind beyond any hope of recovery. In this matter, foreign companies established in Japan are more than willing to help and bring their insight. As was pointed out, Japan already showed its incredible capacity to transform in a blink by relying on foreign expertise during the Meiji era. It might be time for another magic trick of the same kind.

In conclusion, all the attendees agreed that the matter is vast and that we could only scratch it that evening. We parted while already making plans for a greater event on the subject, so keep an eye out for our upcoming “Factory Automation Business Summit” sometime next year, and of course do not miss the Smart Manufacturing Summit in March 2024!

## Thuasne lance une production de masques réutilisables

Avec le développement rapide de l’épidémie de coronavirus, Thuasne a décidé de mobiliser une partie de son outil industriel pour la fabrication de masques réutilisables. En tant que fabricant de dispositifs médicaux spécialisés dans les orthèses, le groupe s’est appuyé sur des matières textiles et des procédés de fabrication déjà maitrisés au sein de l’entreprise pour mettre en place un plan de développement intense et rapide. Les matières premières proviennent de pays européens, déjà en stock ou faciles à approvisionner. Ces masques répondent au guide d’exigences pour les masques barrières (AFNOR SPEC S76-001) publié ce vendredi 27 mars 2020 et tous leurs composants sont certifiés Reach ou OEKO-TEX®. Ils sont filtrants, respirants et sont produits à Saint-Etienne sur un site certifié ISO 9001-13485 (juin 2019).

Issus de la technologie du tissage, ces masques barrières sont destinés à l’usage de personnes saines ne présentant pas de symptôme clinique d’infection virale et n’étant pas en contact avec des personnes présentant de tels symptômes. Ils sont lavables 30 fois à 60°avec un séchage à l’air libre.

# Covid-19 : Point de situation au 10 avril 2020

Source : DG Trésor - Ministère de l'économie et des finances

L’épidémie de Covid-19 a un impact déjà fort sur les économies asiatiques, y compris celle du Japon. Le gouvernement japonais tente de prendre des mesures pour contrer les conséquences graves qui pourraient apparaître à la fois sur le court et long terme. À mesure que l’épidémie se poursuit dans le monde, les plans de soutien économique nippons se multiplient, accompagnés par des mesures financières.

Pour rappel, l’épidémie de Covid-19 touche l’économie japonaise par au moins cinq canaux :

- Une baisse du flux touristique : forte décélération du tourisme chinois depuis fin janvier (pour mémoire, les touristes en provenance de Chine ont représenté 30% des touristes étrangers en 2019 et 40% des recettes touristiques) ; le nombre de visiteurs étrangers au Japon, toutes nationalités confondues, a chuté de 58% en février. Il s’agit de la plus forte baisse enregistrée depuis la catastrophe de Fukushima en 2011.

- Un risque croissant de rupture dans les chaînes d’approvisionnement, en particulier dans l’automobile ou la métallurgie. La Chine a vu ses exportations se replier de 17,2% sur les deux premiers mois de l’année 2020. En conséquence les importations japonaises en provenance de Chine ont connu une chute historique de 47% en février 2020.

- Une baisse des exportations vers la Chine, qui représentaient 19% des exportations nippones en 2019 et 2,7% du PIB du pays. Déjà en retrait sur 2019 (-7,7% par rapport à 2018), sur fond de ralentissement de la croissance chinoise, les exportations du Japon ont diminué en rythme annuel de 1% en février 2020. Il s’agit du 15 ème mois de baisse consécutive.

- Un recul de la confiance des ménages japonais qui pourrait affecter la consommation privée (56% du PIB nippon). Particulièrement résiliente sur les trois premiers trimestres 2019, celle-ci a fortement baissé sur le 4 ème trimestre, à la suite de l’augmentation de la TVA en octobre 2019.

- Un risque de ralentissement de l’activité économique mondiale , avec un impact économique du Covid-19 vraisemblablement supérieur à celui du SRAS (l’économie chinoise pesant 17% du PIB mondial en 2019 contre 6% en 2002).

Au fur et à mesure de l’avancée de l’épidémie, ce ne sont plus seulement les secteurs du tourisme, de la vente, de l’événementiel et du transport aérien qui sont touchés, mais l’ensemble de l’économie qui entrerait en récession. La décision, prise le 7 avril, de déclarer l’état d’urgence et de limiter les déplacements de la population - confinement léger et volontaire « à la japonaise » – exercera un impact négatif supplémentaire sur le 2ème trimestre. Nomura a révisé de -0,2% à -4,8% la croissance japonaise en 2020 tandis que BNP Paribas a évalué l’impact d’un confinement d’un mois à Tokyo à -0,7 point de PIB annuel.

## 1. Un plan gonflé par d'anciennes mesures mais une somme tout de même historique

# Crêpes party in Kansai for Candlemas

Today is Candlemas, a traditional Christian feast day, which most people in France associate with eating crêpes.

It is customary in France to eat crêpes with your family and/or friends for Candlemas , so it is very naturally that we organized a crêpes party at the office yesterday, February 1.

It is always a good occasion to gather people for a warm evening among our residents in Dojima Avanza . This year however, it was all the more special thanks to the generous sponsorship of two partners : Nichifutsu Shōji from Kobe and Yamasan from Kyoto.

Nichifutsu Shōji is a company specialized in supplying many high-quality base ingredients from France for restaurants and hotels (like doughs or chocolate). They also happen to have a retail grocery store Bon App' in Sannomiya, where you can find many goods usually impossible to source in Japan, like high quality jams with rare flavors.

On this special occasion, we were lucky enough to have special jams that are usually not actually available, but that we were authorized to use in our crêpes : rhubarbe, pêche de vigne and Framboise (raspberries)/chocolate. The taste is strong and brings you right back to those childhood memories the way the proverbial madeleine of Proust does.

Then there was Yamasan , a company in Uji, Kyoto that specialized in traditional, highly-concentrated and high-quality matcha tea. They provided a wide array of products, among which we used the matcha powder designed for baking, which we could mix in the dough to make a matcha flavored version of our usual crêpes.

In addition, there was a matcha chocolate that we could make into a ganache to fill the crêpes, and we were also given a sakura powder (not sweetened) that would give a nice sakura taste and color to the whip cream and ganache we mixed with seasonal strawberries.

In this new episode of our Business series Cross Perspectives, we meet Le Wagon Tokyo, the Japanese campus of the renowned French coding bootcamp. Established in 2017, Le Wagon has trained more than 1,100 students in nearly nine years, becoming a key reference for those seeking a career change into tech in Japan.

« Before launching the campus, I met almost 200 people between 2013 and 2016. That network changed everything: I never felt like I was building a company in Japan, but rather within an international micro-ecosystem. »

An international journey turned entrepreneurial engine Before moving to Japan, Pierre spent ten years in Vietnam, where he helped build and scale a web-outsourcing company from 5 to 300 employees. Frequent business trips to meet Japanese clients gradually sparked his interest in the country. In 2016, he decided to take the leap and relocate to Japan to open a representative office, eventually meeting a future co-founder and launching Le Wagon Tokyo. It marked the start of a new entrepreneurial chapter, this time fully his own, in a country he was still learning to navigate.

Starting a business in Japan: simple administration, complex banking Contrary to common perceptions, setting up a company in Japan was not the hardest part. “Incorporating the company took us about one month,” Pierre recalls. The real hurdles came afterward: securing a corporate bank account, dealing with local administrative nuances, and understanding the visa system. Yet, the strong network built over several years helped bypass many obstacles and accelerate the creation of the campus.

# Decline in the ratio of job vacancies to job applications

The ratio between job supply and demand fell in fiscal 2023, the first time in three years.

With many industries facing severe labor shortages , the ratio of job offers to job demands declined in fiscal 2022.

According to a report published by the Ministry of Labor on April 30, the ratio averaged 1.29 for the year ending March: a drop of 0.02 points compared to fiscal 2022. This ratio means that there are 129 vacancies for every 100 applicants.

The average number of jobseekers rose by 0.1% compared to FY2022, reaching 1.92 million per month, while the average number of active job offers fell by 1.6% to around 2.47 million.

Masahiko Yamada, Director General of the Ministry of Labor's Employment Security Bureau, explained this phenomenon by companies’ investments in labor-saving technologies .

Rising material prices may also be behind the decline in this ratio, particularly in the manufacturing and construction sectors.

Unemployment averaged 2.6% in fiscal 2023, unchanged from the previous year.

# Discover the experience sharing of Benjamin Costa, Japan Director of La Maison du Chocolat.

## A business leader with extensive experience bridging French and Japanese cultures answers our questions.

Mr Costa has been the Japan Director of La Maison du Chocolat for three and a half years. La Maison du Chocolat is a French high end chocolate company established in Japan since 1998.

He chose to take on this challenge in order to contribute to the development of a French company in Japan, while benefiting from a certain level of operational freedom, allowing better adaptation to the specificities of the Japanese market.

Today, the brand relies on a team of over one hundred employees and operates ten boutiques located in major cities across Japan. While online sales and corporate gifting also play an important role, the company’s core business remains its retail stores, in a country where the sense of service is truly a way of life.

Key development insights for a retail company in Japan

The brand, now very popular in Japan, has successfully adapted to local consumption habits. However, competition in this market is intense, and it is essential to constantly identify new trends in order to remain attractive, particularly to younger consumers. Launching a new collection every season is essential, but it is not sufficient on its own. To expand the customer base, an evolving and flexible marketing strategy is also required.

More generally, the retail sector is highly trend driven .

At the head of the company, Mr Costa works with an entirely Japanese team. From his arrival, he sought to involve his employees more closely in decision making, not only in how objectives should be implemented, but also in defining the best way to achieve them.

The working culture in Japan, as well as consumer expectations, differ significantly from those in other markets. As a result, relying on the skills and perspective of Japanese team members is essential to successfully develop the business.

# Discover the experience sharing of Benjamin Costa, Japan Director of La Maison du Chocolat.

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/decouvrez-le-partage-dexperience-de-benjamin-costa-directeur-japon-de-la-maison-du-chocolat.html
The working culture in Japan, as well as consumer expectations, differ significantly from those in other markets. As a result, relying on the skills and perspective of Japanese team members is essential to successfully develop the business.

From a management perspective, it is important to show employees that their opinions matter and to support them in bringing their ideas forward. They must be encouraged to propose new initiatives, which is not always easy in a country that values stability and tends to avoid risks associated with change. Progress must be gradual, and it is through a series of small wins that change takes hold, allowing what was once considered “not possible” to become possible.

Mr Costa explained that he began with quick wins , such as obtaining approval from headquarters to change the color of a packaging box that had long been considered untouchable. This helped demonstrate that parts of the product range could be adjusted when supported by strong arguments. Thanks to these small successes , his teams gradually began to put forward new ideas.

- Decision making :

In Japan, decision making to validate a project can take up to ten times longer , as Japanese stakeholders need to review and approve every detail, sometimes repeatedly, before moving forward.

To keep discussions progressing and avoid endless intermediate meetings, Mr Costa summarizes the key decision points by email. This approach helps streamline exchanges and ensures that only the most essential meetings are held.

He also seeks to optimize collaboration by confirming, at the end of each meeting, that the next steps are clearly understood and that timelines are fully aligned. The objective is not to move as quickly as in France, but rather to reduce project and planning cycles as much as possible, from discussion and validation through to implementation .

# Discover the experience sharing of Benjamin Costa, Japan Director of La Maison du Chocolat.

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/decouvrez-le-partage-dexperience-de-benjamin-costa-directeur-japon-de-la-maison-du-chocolat.html
- Future challenges :

Regardless of the sector, it is important to note that the Japanese have a highly developed sense of service but a commercial mindset that is quite different from ours, if not relatively underdeveloped. In retail, it is still common to see many sales staff in stores, but this does not necessarily mean greater efficiency, often due to a lack of training. However, with the challenges of an aging population and low birth rates, mindsets will need to evolve by drawing inspiration from practices abroad, with the aim of optimizing workforce size. Training will therefore become a key issue in the future, in order to manage increasingly lean teams.

Retail in the agri food sector : logistics and distribution channels

The brand’s chocolates are produced in France, where the core know how is located. However, there is also a pastry workshop in Tokyo, notably for the production of éclairs. The company has chosen to import its products directly and relies on a freight forwarder to handle all customs procedures, which are undoubtedly among the strictest in the world .

The brand is present in major department stores such as Hankyu, Newoman, Matsuya and Takashimaya, the Japanese equivalents of Galeries Lafayette in France. These venues remain a safe and effective channel for the development of luxury brands, as they enhance brand image and offer strong customer traffic, but competition is extremely intense.

In the agri food retail sector, having a physical presence is essential. Visual appeal matters, and tasting and product presentation also play a crucial role.

It is important to keep in mind that some importers look for brands to create a short term buzz, and that one year later their commercial efforts may shift in favor of a new product. As a result, it is often necessary to have a local representative to support the importer when choosing this distribution channel.

As for e commerce, it remains a limited channel for the agri food sector , accounting for only 3 percent of turnover in this segment, even though Japan is the fourth largest e-commerce market in the world.

With this channel, it is essential to ensure strong logistics services. For example, Yamato is a reliable partner for delivery.

Foresight

# Despite the yen's weakness, is Japan still an attractive country for foreign workers?

90% of foreigners working in Japan say they want to stay, despite the depreciation of the yen.

A survey carried out by the Japanese company Mynavi revealed that over 90% of foreign workers currently interviewed in Japan wished to continue working there after the expiry of their current visa.

Although this figure is high, it represents a drop compared to the company's survey conducted in 2022. In fact, 5.7% of those surveyed said they did not want to continue working in Japan.

The main reason for this is the depreciation of the yen (40% of respondents), which has reduced the income of foreign workers once converted into their home currency.

Poor working conditions, with long hours of overtime and poor economic prospects, are also a factor in Japan's attractiveness to foreign workers.

“Japan's declining attractiveness to foreign talent is becoming a reality,” said Motoki Yuzuriha, President of Mynavi Global. For him, “companies need to improve wages and other benefits and, at the same time, create workplaces where foreign and Japanese workers can work well together.”

# Discover the beauty of Japanese tradition with Bonjour Matsue

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/discover-the-beauty-of-japanese-tradition-with-bonjour-matsue.html
# Discover the beauty of Japanese tradition with Bonjour Matsue

Matsue City organized a workshop focused on Japanese confectionery and matcha preparation.

| ※This is an event organized by Matsue-city. As spring graces Matsue Castle with an enchanting display of cherry blossoms in full bloom, we invite you to partake in a truly inspiring experience—a Japanese confectionery-making workshop that promises to delight your senses. Dive into the essence of Japanese culture as you create your own Matcha, and savor the satisfaction of enjoying the very tea you have crafted with your own hands. In Matsue, tea is a big part of daily life. Even though the Japanese tea ceremony is often perceived as a formal and codified activity, the local tea culture is simple and open to everyone. People usually drink tea twice a day during the dedicated « tea time » (around 10 am and 3 pm). In the local supermarket, it is not unusual to find some high-quality matcha and Japanese traditional sweets (wagashi) that are used as a side dish to balance the tea’s bitterness. The daily ritual unfolds simply: boil the water, pour it into a bowl, stir the matcha, and savor it while relaxing. A key figure in this tradition is Harusato Matsudaira, known as Fumaï, the 7th lord of Matsue during the Edo period. He promoted tea ceremonies as an art of hospitality, making them welcoming and accessible. His influence led to the annual "Matsue Castle Grand Tea Ceremony," one of Japan's significant tea festivals. Matsue is also known for its wagashi artisans, alongside Kyoto and Kanazawa. Visitors can discover how they are made in one of the many historic shops of the castle town. We invite you to stop by Matsue and enjoy tea just like Fumaï envisioned: open to everyone, simple, and a perfect way to unwind. # EBC - Results of the Flash Survey on the impact of the entry ban on European and American companies and their Japanese partners

The objective of this survey is to better understand the current situation among European and American companies operating in Japan confronted by the entry restrictions due to the COVID-19 crisis and to highlight the direct impact on their economic activity as well as on their Japanese partners.

This survey was designed by the European Business Council in Japan (EBC) and sent to the 15 European National Chambers of Commerce in Japan, who circulated it among their members between June 15 and July 7. The American Chamber of Commerce in Japan (ACCJ) also circulated the survey among its Commercial Membership Representative Members from June 17 to June 25.

325 European and American companies, with headquarters based in 19 European countries, Japan, and the United States, responded. The data was collected anonymously.

Since May 2020, and except for a short period between 1 October 2020 and 7 January 2021, it has been very difficult if not almost impossible for foreign new expatriates or experts to enter Japan. As a result, many respondents report that they lack key personnel and specialists from abroad and current projects have been suspended or new projects cannot be developed, leading to production delays and the cancellation of foreign direct investments into Japan. Companies’ Japanese clients and partners have also been financially impacted.

• 68% of the surveyed foreign companies say that the impact of the entry restrictions on their Japanese customers or partners is significant.

• 12% of respondents estimated that the financial impact on their company’s customers and partners could be over ¥500 million, and 18% of respondents estimated the impact could be between ¥10 million - ¥50 million.

• 71% of respondents say their business plans involve the use of overseas specialists, most of whom have been unable to enter Japan.

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/european-industry-in-japan-heavily-affected-by-the-re-entry-ban-on-non-japanese-citizens.html
COVID-19 • Analyses & Studies

# European industry in Japan heavily affected by the (re-)entry ban on non-Japanese citizens

The European Business Council in Japan (EBC), in cooperation with the various national European Chambers in Japan, has carried out a survey to understand the current situation of European companies in Japan.

The result is clear. According to the answers, 85% of European companies are negatively affected by the ban. Mainly affected is the ability to successfully carry out new or existing projects due to management and/or specialists not being able to (re-)enter Japan. 44% of responders expect a loss in revenue solely due to the (re-)entry ban.

Furthermore, the management of European subsidiaries in Japan cannot travel to the headquarters in Europe causing disruptions to the governance of the companies. Moreover, according to the survey, companies are suffering as leadership and expert positions cannot be filled as non-Japanese personnel cannot enter Japan despite having the proper visas.

In addition, 65% of companies that use Japan as a regional headquarter express problems with management not being able to visit subsidiaries in other countries, eg. South Korea, Taiwan and the Philippines. Unfortunately, the current situation is in direct opposition to Japan’s wish for more foreign companies to use Japan as their regional hub.

Michael Mroczek, the EBC President, said at a press conference that despite the good start of the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement, we are now at risk of losing the momentum due to the (re-)entry ban.

Further, the EBC has been approached by various European companies concerned that the current travel restrictions are unfairly interfering in proper management of European investments in Japan. This is of concern as under various treaties, such as the Free Trade Agreement between Japan and Switzerland and the Energy Charter Treaty, claims may be filed directly against the Government of Japan when fair and equitable treatment is denied to foreign investors.

Furthermore, the (re-)entry ban of permanent and long-term residents may be in breach Article 12 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which clearly states that “[n]o one shall be arbitrarily deprived of the right to enter his own country.”

# Event recap: At the heart of French–Japanese cooperation in Gunma

On December 3rd, the CCIFJ Gunma Desk had the pleasure of hosting a new event focused on French–Japanese cooperation.

On Wednesday, December 3rd, the Gunma Desk of the CCI France-Japan (CCIFJ) had the pleasure of hosting a new event dedicated to strengthening Franco-Japanese cooperation, bringing together around twenty participants.

The event, “Envisioning Gunma’s Future through Franco-Japanese Economic Cooperations” took place in Netsugen , on the 32nd floor of the Gunma Prefectural Office in Maebashi.

The first part of the event featured a seminar led by the Fondation France-Japon (FFJ), an academic foundation affiliated with EHESS (School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences) and conducting research on France and Japan in the field of social sciences. Sébastien Lechevalier , President of the FFJ, introduced several development perspectives for Gunma based on the foundation’s research, focusing on three key themes: population aging, innovation, and regional development.

His presentation was followed by remarks from Bernard Delmas , Honorary Chairman of the CCIFJ and co-chair of the “FFJ Circle”. Drawing on his experience at Michelin in both Auvergne and Gunma, he provided insightful comparisons between the two regions and highlighted their similarities. He also introduced a concrete example of Franco-Japanese cooperation: the Michelin Cities International Network , to which Clermont-Ferrand and Maebashi both belong.

Mayuko Yamamoto , in charge of international relations at the FFJ, then shared her perspective as a Japanese researcher in France. She emphasized that regional areas such as Gunma often serve as fertile ground for innovation, with peripheral territories offering unique conditions for new initiatives.

To conclude, the speakers highlighted how international cooperation, particularly Franco-Japanese collaboration, can offer valuable opportunities for Gunma’s future. Beyond existing initiatives such as those led by the CCIFJ or the Franco-Japanese Association of Gunma , further potential lies in partnerships with French regions, cities, and universities.

The CCIFJ welcomed Hogan Assessments on October 29, 2025, for an exploration of leadership styles between France and Japan.

“Bridging Perspectives: Leadership Lessons Between France and Japan” , featuring Dr. Ryne Sherman , Chief Science Officer.

During the event, Hogan shared key insights from its extensive database, comparing the personalities and leadership styles of Japanese and French executives. While these two cultures approach leadership differently, the results revealed surprising points of convergence in values, decision-making, and teamwork.

The session offered to 40 professionals; HR, business leaders, and international decision-makers a fresh, data-driven perspective on the essentials of effective cross-cultural leadership.

Rather than a formal lecture, the goal was to stimulate reflection and dialogue . Following the presentation, participants continued the conversation during a networking cocktail .

Anne-Marie Paiement , Regional Manager at Hogan Assessments:

“We were delighted to collaborate with the CCI France Japan for this event dedicated to intercultural leadership. This gathering fostered rich and constructive exchanges among professionals from diverse backgrounds, highlighting the importance of understanding and valuing different managerial approaches in a globalized world.”

About Hogan Assessments

A pioneer and global leader in applied personality science for the business world, Hogan Assessments helps organizations select the right talent, develop employees, build effective leaders, and achieve measurable results in 56 countries and 47 languages.

With over 40 years of scientifically validated research , Hogan was the first company to measure personality in a professional context and remains a worldwide reference today.

# Event recap : Wagashi workshop

On Sunday, July 13th, the Chubu Desk of the CCIFJ had the pleasure of welcoming around ten participants to attend a demonstration by Mr. Nobuharu Okamoto, master wagashi artisan from Kotoyo confectionery house.

Globally recognized for his expertise, Mr. Okamoto regularly travels the world to share the delicate art of wagashi, a tradition that has been passed down in his family for over 100 years.

On this exclusive small-scale event, around ten participants including several long-time members of the French community in Nagoya, as well as Japanese guests curious to discover this traditional practice gathered in a warm and friendly atmosphere.

After a live demonstration with commentary on several of his confectionery techniques, Mr. Okamoto surprised the participants by crafting a wagashi blindfolded, a striking display of the precision and mastery he has developed over the years.

This was followed by a hands-on workshop, during which each participant had the opportunity to try their hand at making wagashi, guided step by step by the master.

The workshop concluded on a sweet note, with a tasting of the pastries created by the participants with a serving of matcha tea, in an warm and lively atmosphere.

The CCIFJ Nagoya extends its sincere thanks to Mr. Okamoto for his generosity and dedication, as well as to all participants for their presence and enthusiasm.

We also wish to thank Julie Baud (@tonarinojuri), a tour guide based in Nagoya and actively involved in promoting traditional Japanese arts, for honoring us with her presence on this occasion.

We look forward to seeing you at our upcoming events in Nagoya!

# Event recap : Wegrow “Boosting Growth & Efficiency with Smart AI Collaboration”

On November 13, 2025, the CCIFJ hosted a presentation by Wegrow on the theme of performance and efficiency in business through the use of AI.

Event Highlights

This event brought together 50 leaders and experts to discuss the performance drivers enabled by AI and the sharing of best practices.

Speakers Jean-Louis Cadart, Florent Defontis, and Tristan Helle presented how collaborative AI helps break down organizational silos, improve operational efficiency, and accelerate ROI.

The evening concluded with an interactive quiz, two bottles of champagne at stake, which provided a fun way to recap the key takeaways, followed by a networking session over a buffet.

About Wegrow

Founded in 2018, Wegrow is an AI-enhanced collaborative platform that helps organizations capture, structure, and share their best practices to improve operational performance.

The company now has around 45 employees and supports major international organizations such as L’Oréal, Sephora, Campari Group, Decathlon, Schneider Electric, Franprix, and Pierre Fabre, who trust Wegrow to strengthen the efficiency and engagement of their teams. Wegrow is present in more than 65 countries and has over 30,000 users.

The platform is built on three key pillars to turn internal knowledge into concrete impact:

- Harvest – Capture and structure operational knowledge

- Match – Recommend the right practice to the right person at the right time

- Scale – Turn knowledge into measurable, trackable action

Thanks to this structured, AI-driven approach, Wegrow enables organizations to identify what works, spread it more quickly, and foster a lasting culture of collaboration, generating real, measurable business impact.

For more information: https://www.wegrow-app.com/

Acknowledgments

# Baccarat's Master-Class at the Fukuoka Chamber of Commerce: Branding of a Centuries Old Luxury Brand

Fukuoka's CCI hosted yesterday Mr. Yoshikazu Yann GAHIER's conference on Baccarat Pacific's branding strategies, co-organized by the CCIFJ.

Yesterday, July 26, 2023 in Fukuoka, it was a little over 70 participants who had the opportunity to attend the presentation of a centuries-old French company: Baccarat.

The event started with a Japanese presentation of the CCIFJ's activities by the West Japan area manager. Then Mr. Yoshikazu Yann Gahier, President of Baccarat Pacific, who is also a member of the Chamber's Board of Administrators, opened his speech with a historical retrospective of the company. An attentive audience learned a lot about the history of the "cristal of kings", which is synonym of luxury and elegance since 1764. We also learned that the company accounts for 15 Meilleurs Ouvriers de France (MOF, Best Craftsmen of France, a high distinction) among its qualified makers.

The speech began with a few words in French to surprise the Japanese attendees and get their attention. Then, Mr. Gahier did a brilliant Japanese presentation of the strategies developed by Baccarat over the past 40 years in the country to bring the brand from a status of near unawareness to one of the main references of French luxury.

# Exhibition TENNIS LEGENDS starts on october

Tokyu Corporation, Den-en Tennis Club and CCIFJ are pleased to present a solo exhibition by French photographer GOVIN SOREL.

To mark the 90th anniversary of the Den-en Tennis Club, the artist GOVIN SOREL is exhibiting twelve unpublished photographs featuring portraits of the great players who have marked the history of tennis, including the ‘sworn enemies’ Björn Borg and John Mc Enroe in a single shot. But also, both finalists of the 1983 tournament; Yannick Noah from France and Mats Wilander from Sweden. This exhibition will be held from October 1-31, 2024 at the Denen Tennis Club, one of the most famous tennis clubs in Japan's tennis history!

Focusing on Rolland Garros' 1995 Legends Trophy, the exhibition photographs capture not just individual beauty but also embody the collective story. Without the pressure of the professional circuit, all the players gathered after the matches at the Villa Barclay near the Champs Élysées to celebrate their meeting again.

GOVIN SOREL's fascination with the notion of identity, and with his work, is now at the heart of this exhibition. The twelve portraits, staged in a theatrical and poetic manner, bear witness to a collective identity. As such, each of these twelve black and white portraits calls for a cross-representation between the man and the sportsman, substituting their athletic past with an object.

This approach, which puts the sportsman, his mischief and sometimes his skill, under the microscope, leads to deep down to tennis' essence. What excites in competition, beyond the intense stakes, if not the athlete, is his personality, his otherness.

That through which a sport brings to the highest what it is, the alliance of strength and grace. All the shots were taken with a Polaroid 4x5 sheet film, as a one-shot, to leave them free to strike their pose, without any direction, blurring all boundaries between professional and private life.

# Exploring Japan’s Leather Industry in Himeji

An Immersive Visit to a Traditional Japanese Tannery in the Heart of Hyōgo Prefecture

Not everyone has the chance to step inside a tannery, especially one that preserves an ancestral craft dating back over 1,000 years: the production of Himeji white leather .

On April 8, we had the privilege of offering an exclusive behind-the-scenes experience to around fifteen lucky participants at the Sanyo Leather tannery. This unique opportunity was made possible thanks to Mr. Emmanuel Marchat , Board Member of the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCIFJ) and Managing Director of Stahl Japan .

Stahl is a global leader in the production of chemical agents used notably in leather processing. Long considered a polluting industry, leather manufacturing has undergone a significant transformation in recent decades, thanks in part to the growing use of water-based , more environmentally friendly solutions, many developed by Stahl. Sanyo Leather is in fact the second tannery in Japan to have received the LWG environmental certification .

#### Understanding the Leather-Making Process

The day began with a seminar presented by Mr. Marchat, who gave a detailed overview of the leather production process:

- Cleaning : Soaking in lime and acid baths to remove impurities, soften, and prepare the hides

- Tanning : Using tannin or chrome, this step gives leather its key properties and durability

- Dyeing : The leather is refined, dyed, and stretched

- Drying : A crucial step to stabilize the material

- Finishing : Sanding, polishing, painting (which affects only the surface, unlike dye which penetrates the entire thickness), ironing, and embossing (which gives the leather its final texture)

We then had the opportunity to tour the tannery and observe each of these steps firsthand. Sanyo Leather stands out as one of the few tanneries in Japan to still manage the entire production process in-house—from receiving the raw hides to finishing the leather.

# Exploring Japan’s Leather Industry in Himeji

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/exploring-japans-leather-industry-in-himeji.html
Mr. Marchat also emphasized a little-known fact: leather production is a circular activity that adds value to a by-product of the food industry. Indeed, the hides used come almost exclusively from meat consumption.

#### A Moment of Conviviality

The day continued with a relaxed lunch in Himeji Castle Park under the blooming cherry blossoms—a chance for participants to share their impressions and strengthen professional ties in an informal setting.

To round off the experience, part of the group enjoyed a self-guided tour of Himeji Castle, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, adding a cultural touch to an already rich and engaging day.

A heartfelt thank you to all participants for their presence and interest, and to Mr. Emmanuel Marchat for his commitment and invaluable insights.

# EY European Attractiveness Survey 2023

France continues to maintain its position as the leading European country in attracting foreign investment, with nearly 1,260 projects registered in 2022, marking the fourth consecutive year of this achievement. This remarkable feat sets a historic record and comes as encouraging news just before the sixth edition of the Choose France summit. This exclusive event, scheduled for 15th May, is specifically designed for top executives from major foreign companies and will take place at the prestigious Château de Versailles, following an invitation extended by the President of the French Republic.

France is the most attractive country in Europe in 2022

France maintains its position as the most attractive country in Europe in 2022, according to a survey conducted by EY. Despite the challenging geopolitical, economic, and social environment, France has even extended its lead over its traditional competitors, the UK and Germany.

The survey revealed that France recorded 1,259 announced implementations or expansions in 2022, representing a 3% increase compared to the previous year. This achievement marks the fourth consecutive year that France has topped the European ranking. EY attributes this ongoing success to the continued positive momentum that started in 2017, despite economic challenges stemming from geopolitical crises.

EY's findings indicate that the desire to invest in France remains strong, with 61% of surveyed companies having immediate investment plans in the country for 2023. Decision-makers closely scrutinize France's economic, social, and energy landscape, anticipating potential changes in the short term that could impact future results.

An upturn for all French regions

A positive trend can be observed in all regions of France, with each region benefiting from its attractive status. The Ile-de-France region, with 326 projects in 2022, has secured the top spot in the ranking of the most attractive regions in Europe, surpassing Greater London (299 projects in 2022) for the first time in the history of the EY survey.

# Facing rising prices, more and more Japanese are opting for the suburbs

As property prices continue to soar in Japan, almost 17,000 people have left Tokyo to settle in the suburbs.

The “ datsu tokyo ” movement (脱・東京) is gaining momentum in the Japanese capital due to rising property prices. Last year, almost 17,000 people left Tokyo for outlying prefectures.

Published by the Ministry of the Interior, a report shows how the prefectures of Tokyo, Kanagawa, Saitama and Chiba are experiencing an over-migration of 20-year-olds to Tokyo. However, people in their thirties and forties, the generation that raises children, prefer to emigrate to outlying regions.

With rising rental prices, the generation raising children is struggling to find housing in Tokyo: a report published by the Cabinet Office indicates a shift “to suburbs of the Tokyo metropolitan area, where housing prices are lower.”

The same report stresses the need to “guarantee housing for the generation raising children by promoting supply-side measures, such as increasing the supply of public housing.”

The lack of affordable housing is therefore yet another obstacle for families, in a country characterized by a falling birth rate and an aging population.

# Fauchon grocery announced buyout by Galapagos group

The famous grocery store on rue de la Madeleine in Paris has been acquired by the Breton Galapagos group.

Fauchon has been acquired by Galapagos, headed by Jérôme Tacquard .

“There is a lot in common between the two entities, a sharing of values and an anchoring in French haute gastronomy,” he explains in an interview with the newspaper Ouest France .

The Fauchon grocery store is known as the emblem of Place Madeleine in Paris , but also for its stores all over the world. However, the brand has been weakened by the health crisis.

The Galapagos group is famous for its Biscuits roses de chez Fossier, Gavottes (crêpes dentelles) and Traou Mad (cookies), and also owns Mademoiselle de Margaux and Moulin du Pivert (organic cookies). It generates annual sales of close to 125 million euros.

This acquisition will strengthen Galapagos’ international presence : Fauchon is present in over 15 countries with more than 80 points of sale, and also runs two 5-star hotels (Paris and Kyoto).

“We already generate 20% of our sales internationally, and the arrival of Fauchon in the family group, with its strong synergies, will enable us to pursue this development and continue to promote France and its gourmet products,” commented Jérome Tacquard .

# Félix Portier, CCIFJ Ambassador for Hokkaido

As General Manager of NASKEO Kankyo KK, the Japanese subsidiary of the Keon Group, Félix Portier works from Sapporo to develop anaerobic digestion solutions tailored to the needs of farms and wastewater treatment plants. With nearly ten years of experience in Hokkaido, he now draws on his local knowledge to strengthen ties between French and Japanese companies.

A career between France and Japan

After studying Japanese at Toulouse II - Jean Jaurès University, including a year as an exchange student at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa, Félix Portier obtained his master’s degree in 2015. He subsequently worked in a variety of fields, from translation and interpreting to manual work, before joining NASKEO in 2017 through the French International Internship Programme (V.I.E.) as a site coordinator on an anaerobic digestion project in Hokkaido. He later moved into business development before becoming Managing Director of NASKEO Kankyo KK in August 2025, following the acquisition of stakes in the company by two Hokkaido-based groups.

Anaerobic digestion in support of the energy transition

Based in Sapporo, he oversees the deployment of Biolectric® micro-anaerobic digestion units, which enable livestock farms to convert their organic waste into renewable energy. Operating at the intersection of agriculture and the energy transition, this business allows him to build close relationships with local stakeholders. In January 2026, NASKEO Kankyo notably received the Jury’s Special Award at the French Business Awards (FBA), organized by the CCIFJ, and won the Hokkaido GX New Energy Award.

# For its 100th anniversary, Gucci opens a pop-up exhibition in a historical Kyoto Machiya

For its 100th anniversary, a Kyoto Machiya (Japanese townhouse) has been transformed into the Gucci Bamboo House – in honor of the brand’s iconic bag.

The pop-up is in celebration of the brand’s 100th anniversary and highlights the latest collection titled ‘Aria’ by creative director Alessandro Michele.

As Gucci frequently draws inspiration from the past to create new and innovative pieces, Kyoto – revered for its deeply rooted traditions – was a fitting destination to showcase the new collection.

Installations include the brand’s bags with classic bamboo handles while also showing the craftsmanship behind the process.

The library is especially eye-catching with flower-print wallpaper, Gucci chairs and curated bookshelves reminiscent of the Gucci Garden Bookstore in Florence, Italy. Other details, like the shoji paper panels with Gucci monogram, are far more subtle. There is also a salon displaying the reissued Gucci Diana bag.

As a nod to the brand’s latest series of handbags – a revival of the bamboo-handled purses Gucci first released in 1947 – the house is now monikered as the Gucci Bamboo House. This theme is consistent throughout the machiya, which is not only decorated with bamboo furnishings and installations but also boasts a lush bamboo grove in its private Japanese garden.

The Gucci Bamboo House is now open through August 15. Admission is free, but visitors must make reservations in advance.
