# Looking Back at the 2026 France–Japan Economic Forum in Fukuoka, Kyushu Desk

Mr. Bernard Delmas's exceptional intervention sparked fruitful discussions and valuable exchanges among participants.

On May 28, the CCIFJ 2026 Economic Forum in Fukuoka provided an opportunity for rich discussions and valuable exchanges during an exceptional presentation by Bernard Delmas . This edition brought together around sixty participants around the theme: “Supporting Companies Beyond Borders: Global Leadership Through the Experiences of Michelin and Nissan .”

Following a brief presentation of the Chamber’s activities by our Director of Regional Offices, we had the privilege of welcoming Bernard Delmas, former executive of Michelin and Nissan Motor Corporation, who generously shared his experience and insights during a particularly engaging and thought-provoking presentation.

Having arrived in Japan in the 1980s, Bernard Delmas has witnessed firsthand the profound transformations the country has undergone over the past four decades. Drawing on this unique perspective, he highlighted how international leadership relies on a delicate balance between global vision, local adaptation, and intercultural openness. These challenges remain more relevant than ever for companies seeking to expand and thrive internationally.

A question-and-answer session followed, allowing participants to further explore the topics raised during the presentation and gain additional insights into the many questions and concerns facing businesses today. Attendees enthusiastically took advantage of this opportunity to engage directly with the speaker.

Participants highly appreciated the quality of the discussions and continued their conversations during the networking session that followed. This convivial moment, accompanied by coffee and a selection of French pastries that were particularly enjoyed by guests, helped extend the exchanges in a warm and lively atmosphere. The forum concluded at 5:30 p.m., although many participants were still engaged in conversation, already looking forward to future opportunities to meet again.

We would like to extend our warmest thanks to the Fukuoka Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FCCI), with whom we co-organized this forum. Our sincere gratitude also goes to the City of Fukuoka and the Institut français du Kyushu for their valuable support in making this event possible.

# France–Japan Strategic Tech Forum 2026: A Key Event for Franco-Japanese Innovation

AI, Defense & Industrial Sovereignty

On September 24, 2026 , Tokyo will host the France–Japan Strategic Tech Forum 2026 , organized by La French Tech Tokyo in partnership with Alta Ares and Scrum Ventures . The event will bring together more than 150 stakeholders from the French and Japanese tech ecosystems to address issues at the heart of today’s strategic agenda: AI, defense, deeptech and industrial sovereignty .

Through keynotes, panel discussions and networking sessions, the forum aims to foster collaboration between startups, corporations, investors and public-sector stakeholders from France and Japan. Discussions will notably explore emerging trends in technological and industrial sovereignty, the role of AI in strategic sectors, and opportunities for stronger cooperation between the two countries.

The forum is designed for innovative startups, VC and CVC investors, French companies operating in Japan, as well as Japanese corporations looking to strengthen their ties with the French Tech ecosystem.

### A Sponsorship Opportunity for CCIFJ Member Companies

For companies with an interest in AI, cybersecurity, defense, deeptech or industrial innovation , the forum also offers a valuable opportunity to become a partner of the event.

Partners will benefit from increased visibility among a highly qualified audience of business leaders, investors, entrepreneurs and public-sector stakeholders from both France and Japan. Depending on the partnership level, opportunities include speaking or panel participation, enhanced brand visibility, curated introductions and privileged access to participants.

Beyond visibility, sponsorship offers an opportunity to build strategic relationships with innovative startups, investors and corporate partners across the French and Japanese ecosystems.

CCIFJ member companies interested in exploring sponsorship opportunities or learning more about the available partnership packages are invited to contact our team: communication(@)ccifj.or.jp

# Free Webinar: Dr. Jacques Attali, "Intelligence of Europe"; Interpreting Cities, People and the World in the So-Called "With-Corona" Era

Purpose of the symposium

In 2020, the global spread of the novel coronavirus COVID-19 has significantly affected our society and economy.

Looking back at the history since the Industrial Revolution, the period of industrialization and mass production and consumption has been premised on a shift of population from rural to urban areas; in other words "sparse population" to "dense population." Every business activity in recent years, from office buildings and retail facilities to restaurants, is based on "volume" associated with "dense crowds."

That assumption has collapsed due to the fear of the novel coronavirus COVID-19.

It is no exaggeration to say that this is an event that will remain in the history of humanity, as we started calling it "BC/AC" (Before Corona/After Corona) to mark the end/beginning of the history. Since it takes a certain amount of time to develop a vaccine, it is inevitable to coexist with COVID-19.

Even if we manage to overcome COVID-19, the battle between humans and infectious diseases will still continue, given that there are a large number of unexpected infectious diseases in the nature.

How will our society and economy, and the world change in the era of "With-Corona"? In these days, in which national particularism can make a profit, how can humankind deal with global issues such as infectious diseases and global warming?

At this symposium, we would like to examine the answers to that questions together with the French thinker and economist, Dr. Jacques Attali, who is also referred to as "Intelligence of Europe." Then, we will discuss with experts including Dr. Attali, Prof. Kazunari Uchida, Prof. Kengo Kuma and Prof. Seiichiro Yonekura, about the community development and working style in the With-Corona era as well as the possibility of sustainable development goals (SDGs) and public-private partnership (PPP).

# French artist Marion Flament returns to Japan with her first major solo exhibition

Starting December 4, 2025, the Esther Okada Art Gallery in Yoyogi will present Nothing Seems Certain , the first major solo exhibition in Japan by Marion FLAMENT, a 36-year-old French artist renowned for her bold glass creations and striking play of light. The exhibition will run until December 21, 2025.

Her art explores the poetics of the ephemeral and light as a language , revealing the memory of materials and the traces left by time. Between matter, elements, and duration, her work acts as a sensitive revealer, inviting viewers to change their perception of the world .

In Nothing Seems Certain , Marion Flament seeks to materialize impermanence, fragility, and transformation . Her compositions, often minimalist, balance between the organic and the geometric, between chaos and control. More than a visual demonstration, her work offers an emotional and sensory experience , where texture, color, and light interact in subtle harmony.

Her creations invite us to slow down and observe , to rediscover the beauty of details and the hidden richness within the simplicity of matter. Through this approach, Marion Flament offers a poetic counterpoint to the frenetic pace of the modern world – an art of contemplation and resonance.

Born in 1989 in Reims , Marion Flament lives and works in Paris . A graduate of the École Boulle and the École nationale supérieure des arts décoratifs de Paris (EnsAD) , she is a laureate of the Hermès Glass Academy , the Artists’ Foundation , ADAGP , and CNAP . Her work has been showcased in numerous international art residencies and exhibited in Milan, Munich, Hong Kong, Tokyo , and Singapore , confirming her place on the global contemporary art scene.

# French bistro "Loiseau de France" settles in Tokyo

Reflecting the vision of legendary French chef Bernard Loiseau, the Loiseau de France Bistro will open its doors in Tokyo on Sunday, June 2, 2024.

Bérangère Loiseau, CEO of the Bernard Loiseau Group, is delighted to have fulfilled Bernard Loiseau's ambition to return to the cosmopolitan city of Tokyo after three decades of hard work.

On Sunday, June 2, 2024, Tokyo will welcome the opening of Loiseau de France, a new gastronomic adventure inspired by the vision of the renowned French chef Bernard Loiseau. For Bérangère Loiseau, CEO of the group of the same name, this opening is an emotional achievement and a tribute to her father, thirty years after Bernard Loiseau enchanted Japan with his cuisine.

The Loiseau family's ties with Japan go back to the years 1992-1995, when Bernard Loiseau opened a replica of his restaurant "La Côte d'Or" on Rokko Island, Kobe. His cuisine, based on the purity of flavors and simplicity (low fat, low sugar and sauces deglazed with water), immediately captivated Japanese palates.

Loiseau de France will be located at the Institut Français du Japon (IFJ) in Tokyo, a vibrant cultural center managed by the French Embassy and dedicated to promoting the French language and culture. The IFJ, which will be transformed into a "French village" by architect Sou Fujimoto in 2021, surrounded by a lush garden, is the perfect setting for this new bistro.

The restaurant will have three distinct spaces: - A 63-seat bistro dining room. - A snack area with 20 seats and a terrace. - A boutique dedicated to 100% Made in France products.

# Gala Party in Fukuoka : Mathieu Martin shares his Culinary Adventure

Fukuoka, Japan - In culinary world, every travel is an opportunity to discover new flavors and to share unique moments.

Arrived on 9th of June, Mathieu Martin has soon plunged into the vibrante atomosphere of Fukuoka. His first day in the town has started with his walking in the Ohori Park , followed by an immersion into the dynamic areas of Daimyo and Tenjin . The highlight of the day was without doubt the tasting of a traditionnal tonkatsu ramen at a bustling yatai in Nakatsu , offering him a fisrt taste of the richness of the local cuisine.

The morning of 10th June was devoted to the meetings with local producters, guided by Fukuoka town hall. Mathieu began his day by visiting a renowend Wagyu beef breeder, devolving into the subtlety of the breeding of this world-renowned beef.

He then had the unique opportunity to discover edible chrysanthemums ( shungiku ), thanks to a passionate grower, underlining the importance of local agricultural culture in regional cuisine.

Between two explorations, Mathieu also had the pleasure to try the famous mentai furansu , a local speciality that surprised him with its taste. His day ended at Solaria Nishitetsu Hotel , where he shared his expertise with local chefs, while tasting their own innovative creations. Inspired by his morning discoveries, he ended his day with a Wagyu barbecue, celebrating the perfection of the local beef.

Tuesday 11 June was a day dedicated to perfecting details of the dishes in the kitchen. Mathieu Martin worked closely with the team at the Solaria Nishitetsu Hotel to ensure that every dish for the gala the following evening was a true work of culinary art.

# Government calls for “25,000 foreign drivers” in the automotive sector

Due to the aging population, the Japanese government is now opening up the automotive sector to foreign labor.

Faced with labor shortages and a reduction in overtime for truck drivers , the Japanese government relaxed the conditions for accepting foreign workers on March 29.

The “2024 problem” refers to the reduction of overtime for truck drivers, which could lead to a shortage of personnel in the transport and logistics sectors. The government is therefore seeking to alleviate this shortage by bringing in foreign drivers.

Over the next five years, the motor transport industry as a whole (including buses and cabs) will accept up to 24,500 foreign drivers . However, this may not be enough, as the transport sector will be short of almost 200,000 drivers - efforts to find drivers domestically will also remain paramount.

Despite these coming shortages, the number of foreign nationals is fixed every five years under the existence of a specified skills system, which came into being in 2019.

This is divided into two categories: specific skills number 1, which require a “considerable degree of knowledge or experience” and a period of residence not exceeding five years; and specific skills number 2, which require “qualified skills” based on years of professional experience.

The recruitment of truck drivers falls into the first category.

# HORIBA acquires South Korea’s EtaMax to strengthen semiconductor business

HORIBA Group, through its subsidiary HORIBA STEC Korea, has completed the acquisition of South Korean company EtaMax, based in Suwon. EtaMax specializes in wafer inspection systems for the compound semiconductor market.

The company develops equipment using photoluminescence technology to detect microscopic defects and assess wafer uniformity — a key process in the production of next-generation power semiconductors, widely used in electric vehicles and data centers.

With this acquisition, HORIBA aims to integrate its own spectroscopic technologies, such as Raman spectroscopy and ellipsometry, with EtaMax’s software expertise to offer more advanced inspection solutions. The goal is to improve production yields and strengthen quality control for compound semiconductors.

This strategic move aligns with HORIBA’s MLMAP 2028 management plan, which targets ¥235 billion in sales by 2028 in the advanced materials and semiconductor field.

# HORIBA Medical and CEA-Leti Strengthen Their Partnership to Develop Tomorrow’s Diagnostics at the Point of Care

HORIBA Medical et le CEA-Leti poursuivent leur partenariat pour développer le diagnostic de demain, au lit du patient.

HORIBA Medical, a subsidiary of Japan-based HORIBA Group, the global leader for measurement and analysis systems, has been designing, manufacturing and marketing high performance analyzers for laboratories and hospitals for over 30 years. This expertise that has made the company one of the world leaders in Hematology and a key player in the Hemostasis and Clinical Chemistry activity.

Today, patient care and treatment practices are evolving quickly. HORIBA Medical is designing solutions to anticipate patient-centered needs by developing new POCT (Point of Care Testing) systems.

In parallel, for the past six years HORIBA Medical has been working with one of the most innovative organizations in the field of new technologies, CEA-Leti, the technology research laboratory of CEA Tech, federating their respective skills in a Joint Laboratory called HEMACOUNT.

“We focused on two disruptive technologies: a microfluidic cartridge and a new, lens-free imaging device (LensFree), which will enable development of more compact, easier-to-use POCT-type devices,” says Damien Isebe, who heads up this highly innovative project at HORIBA Medical. “Twelve families of patents have been filed since the start of the project, and the latest one has been the subject of several scientific papers”.

“Flow cytometry is the main analytical technology in hematology, but it requires large and complex hardware systems. Conversely, lens-free imaging combined with a sample prepared as a microfluidic cartridge paves the way to a simple and compact disruptive architecture. This imaging technique provides a wide field of view (≈30mm²) resulting in a counting statistic (a few thousand cells) in one single acquisition consistent with required hematological performance,” explains Sophie Morales, laboratory head at CEA-Leti.

# Hotel prices in Japan to rise by 25% between 2022 and 2023

The end of health restrictions and the upturn in tourism have had an impact on accommodation prices.

The price of hotel rooms in Japan in 2023 rose by more than 25% compared with 2022 , according to the latest Consumer Price Index report published by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. This increase is attributed to the lifting of health restrictions and the low yen rates that have led to a strong recovery in tourism since 2023.

According to Takuto Yasuda, researcher at the Nissay Research Institute : “With the end of the Corona and the significant upturn in demand, there is a shortage of staff. Wages have had to be increased in order to acquire labor, and prices are being passed on to hotel bills. There is also a tendency to pass on increased costs due to higher prices to hotel bills .”

The end of the pandemic, the significant upturn in demand and the shortage of manpower in Japan are also having an impact on hotels, which are having to spend money on renovations.

Japan-wide, the impact is also being felt on “business travel.” Many companies are having to increase their flat-rate accommodation costs for employee travel.

# Hummingbag : reusable bags in the land of disposable packaging

Hummingbag designs and manufactures reusable bags made from recyclable materials, tailored to its clients’ needs. The company, based in Hong Kong, decided to enter the Japanese market after a first trip to Tokyo in 2011 : “ We were told that it would be difficult to sell bags in Japan, that our product did not offer enough added value. When we arrived, we immediately noticed the following : bags are mostly intended for single use and are not aesthetic at all. We therefore decided to take our chance .”

In 2012, Hummingbag took part in the Tokyo International Gift Show. There, Cécile Chaigneau, Head of Sales, met the Seijo Ishi group, with whom Hummingbag signed its first sale four months later. Building on this experience, Hummingbag turned to CCI France Japan to structure its development project: “ We found a few clients through our website, but our direct prospecting, without a real command of Japanese and above all without being introduced, led to nothing. We then heard that CCI France Japan could help us save a great deal of time .”

In 2014, after two months of preparation, the team from the Business Support Service of CCI France Japan organized a series of meetings for Hummingbag with fifteen Japanese companies, including major agri food distributors and firms specialized in events and communication. “ I realize how important it is to come and meet your counterparts in Japan. We are not the only ones manufacturing this type of bag, but we arrived at the right time and met the right people. Without CCI France Japan, we probably would not have been able to move forward so quickly ”, explains Cécile Chaigneau.

# Hurry and visit Miss Dior before she escapes!

"Miss Dior spotted in Tokyo": it could be the title of a dispatch, a musical fugue or a novel. The iconic perfume is the subject of Miss Dior, Stories of a Miss, an exhibition at the Roppongi Museum until July 16, in the heart of a Japan that has made the timeless Miss Dior its adopted daughter, so to speak. Miss Dior is Christian's child prodigy. After the war, the French designer left his (pink) mark on fashion history with his creations. But even in his unique world, this fragrance remains singular. The first women's fragrance, in which the designer wanted to combine love and freedom, it has accompanied the House of Dior since its first fashion show in 1947. With stubbornness: Miss Dior is now the world's leading prestige fragrance, according to consultant NPD. It is always in the zeitgeist. And it's got a lot to live up to: it was composed as a tribute to Christian Dior's own sister, Catherine, an early World War II Resistance fighter deported to Ravensbrück. The exhibition showcases Dior treasures never before on public display, such as the typewriter of the great Christian Dior's little sister, original ready-to-wear ensembles from the 60s and famous Haute Couture gowns from the past. It also includes original creations. In particular, the Japanese architect Shohei Shigematsu has created a vertiginous path in the shape of an untied pink ribbon, already used by Dior's contemporary muses: Natalie Portman, Jisoo (Blackpink), Yuko Araki..., Miss Dior, Stories of a Miss manages to capture the elusive Miss Dior. But not for long: the very essence of perfume is to escape. Run to the Roppongi Museum before she takes to the air on July 16.

Duration: Until July 16. 10:00-21:00

# Increase in consumer price index for 2023

The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications has published its latest report on the average consumer price index.

The latest report on the consumer price index (inflation measure) for the year 2023 has been published by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications.

On average, the consumer price index in Japan rose by 2.8% year-on-year (excluding unprocessed fresh food).

This was 0.2 percentage points less than the previous year's increase of 3.0% - the highest level in 41 years, since 1981.

The index for food products (excluding unprocessed fresh foods) rose by 7.5% on the previous year. Among products, the index for eggs rose by 24.5%, for ice cream by 11.6% and for minced steaks in restaurants by 9.2%.

Due to the recovery in tourist demand, prices for accommodation, including hotels, rose by 25.5%.

However, prices for electricity and city gas bills fell by more than 10% respectively.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications said: “In the catering sector, measures have been taken to increase prices due to rising labor costs. We would like to confirm whether the current depreciation of the yen will affect the prices of food and other products .”

Foresight

# Increase in Japanese automobile exports in February

Automobile exports rose by 11.8% in February 2024 compared with February 2023.

The weakening yen is said to be behind the rise in automobile exports in February 2024 . This is the conclusion of a report published on March 29 by the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association. This is the 13th consecutive month of growth.

By vehicle type, cars grew by +17% in February 2024 compared with February 2023, while trucks and buses recorded negative growth (-25.1% and -49.4% respectively).

By region, exports increased to Europe, North America and Oceania (+44.9%, +18.7% and +7.2% respectively). However, exports to Asia, the Middle East and Africa were lower than the previous period.

In January, domestic production had fallen by 7%, the first decline in 13 months.

Foresight

# Increase in the number of foreign tourists in hotels

Hotel stays by foreigners rose by 68% in Japan, reaching a record high in March.

Overnight stays by foreigners in Japanese hotels rose by 68.2% year-on-year to around 12.7 million.

This was the highest monthly figure ever , due in part to the weak yen.

According to the Japan Tourism Association, this latest figure exceeded the previous record of around 12.3 million set in December 2023.

Overnight stays by all travelers (including foreign travelers) were also up 8.2% year-on-year, reaching around 55 million in the reference month.

Tourism in Japan has been on the rebound since the government lifted border controls imposed in the wake of the pandemic, but also thanks to the low level of the yen.

# International Symposium on Planetary Health and the Cycles of Life at The University of Tokyo 2026

From Mechanistic Insights to Future Translation and Innovation

Purpose and focus

How should we live and work to reduce the burden on the planet?

Rethinking healthy life expectancy and working life as tools for environmental sustainability

Today, we face serious global challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and shortages of natural resources. These problems are not only about energy or technology. They are also closely linked to how people live and how people work.

At the same time, advances in medicine, nutrition, and living conditions mean that people can live longer and stay healthier for more years than before. Until now, longer healthy lives and longer working lives have mainly been discussed in terms of personal well-being, social security, or labor shortages.

In this symposium, we take a different perspective.

We ask a simple but important question:Can longer healthy lives and working lives be used as tools to reduce the burden on the planet?

When illness and long-term care are concentrated in the later stages of life, society needs large amounts of medical services, care workers, materials, and energy. This places a heavy burden not only on society but also on the environment. If more people can stay healthy for longer, it may be possible to reduce these pressures and change how resources are used across society.

Working longer does not have to mean producing more and consuming more. It can also mean sharing knowledge, supporting others, caring for communities, and protecting nature. These are forms of work that contribute to society while using fewer resources.

This symposium explores practical ways to extend healthy life expectancy and working life while reducing environmental impact, focusing on the following themes:

- Food: Diets that are good for both human health and the planet

- Physical activity: Everyday movement to maintain health and prevent disease

- Sleep: Improving sleep quality to support mental and physical well-being

- Disease prevention: Preventing illness rather than treating it after it occurs

- Gut microbiota: Living in balance with the microorganisms in our bodies

# Interview with Jean-Marc Peillex: a collaboration between Saint-Gervais and Yamanouchi

Jean-Marc Peillex, Mayor of Saint-Gervais, was in Japan to strengthen a strategic partnership between his town and Yamanouchi. In this interview, he looks back at this collaboration’s origins, aims and prospects.

▶️ 11 minutes ? Language : french - available subtitles : french and english

The birth of the partnership: The partnership between Saint-Gervais and Yamanouchi was born out of opportunities and meetings facilitated by the Lyon consulate. The two towns, which share similarities in profile (ski resorts, thermal baths and mountains), quickly agreed to formalise the agreement. A protocol was signed to develop joint projects in less than a year.

Objectives and initiatives: Jean-Marc Peillex explains that this partnership goes well beyond traditional twinning. The aim is to create cultural and educational exchanges between young people. Initiatives involving schools and municipal children's councils are underway, with planned exchanges. Another crucial area is gastronomy. The two towns want to organise culinary exchanges to promote their local specialities.

Knowledge transfer: Saint-Gervais is contributing its expertise in ski resort management and sustainable development. Jean-Marc Peillex emphasises the importance of limiting excessive infrastructure, consolidating ski lifts and diversifying activities beyond winter to exploit the potential of all four seasons.

Enhancing the value of the area: The mayor stresses the importance of developing a policy centred on the local population. In Saint-Gervais, this approach has helped to stem the rural exodus and increase the permanent population. He encourages Yamanouchi to adopt a similar approach to preserve local life and avoid exclusive dependence on seasonal tourism.

Climate change and snow cover: Although the French Alps are facing increasing challenges from global warming, Yamanouchi still benefits from abundant natural snow cover. Jean-Marc Peillex stresses the importance for Japan of exploiting this opportunity to attract visitors while remaining respectful of the environment.

Although Brittany is not located in central France, it has played a key role in initial Japanese investments in France, particularly in the 1980s when companies like Canon set up their operations.

A special connection between Japan and Brittany: Mr. Girard explains that this connection has deep historical roots. Brittany has always been open to the world, notably through maritime trade. Its ancestors were probably among the first to engage with other cultures and people, establishing historical ties with nations like Japan. He also highlights the shared values between the two regions, such as work ethic, commitment, and respect for promises, which are strong in both Brittany and Japan. A significant example for him is the commitment of Canon's employees in Brittany, which played a pivotal role in the company's decision not to close its factory in the region. Mr. Girard also emphasises the similarities in landscapes between Brittany and Japan, notably their strong connection to the sea and horizon and the importance of regional identity, which is experienced with pride in both cultures.

Personal memories and the arrival of Japanese companies: Mr Girard recalls the arrival of Japanese companies in the 1980s, a time marked by scepticism and fears about the presence of foreign companies, sometimes called "screwdriver factories." Many doubted their true intentions, such as concerns that they might be here solely for tax advantages or to sell their products more effectively. However, trust was established over time, especially given Japan's comparable standard of living to Europe, which helped dispel the fears associated with emerging markets.

Japanese tourism in Brittany: Regarding Japanese tourism, Mr. Girard explains that it remains small but steady, with around 15,000 Japanese visitors coming to Brittany each year. However, most Japanese tourists still prefer other regions in France, such as Paris, Bordeaux, or Mont-Saint-Michel. Although an attractive destination, Brittany has yet to become a must-visit place for Japanese tourists. Mr. Girard stresses the importance of making it easier for Japanese tourists to visit Brittany, encouraging them to cross the Couesnon River to explore places like Cancale, Saint-Malo, and Dinard.

Cuisine and seafood products: Gastronomy, particularly seafood, is another area of convergence between Brittany and Japan. Mr. Girard mentions seaweed, shellfish, and other specific products from Brittany found in Japan. He sees potential for collaboration in exploring these flavours and creating exchanges centred on these culinary products, focusing on adding value to Breton exports.

Economic development and the future of Brittany: In discussing Brittany's economic future, Mr. Girard emphasises the importance of supporting workers in Breton factories owned by Japanese companies while focusing on emerging and innovative sectors. He highlights industries such as hydrogen, space, health, and cybersecurity, where Brittany has many promising companies. He notes that Brittany has a long industrial tradition and continues to invest in strategic sectors.

# Itinéraires singuliers Podcast- From Formula 1 to the political arena: Sakon Yamamoto's unique journey between Japan and the world

From the absolute summit of motorsport to the Japanese national political stage, Sakon Yamamoto’s path illustrates a rare trajectory, shaped by competition, international experience, and a strong sense of commitment. A trajectory whose origins can be traced back to a decision made at the age of ten. In this episode of the Itinéraires Singuliers podcast, we welcome the former Formula 1 driver and former member of the House of Representatives to reflect on a journey where speed, risk, and responsibility constantly intersect.

Born in Toyohashi, in Aichi Prefecture, Sakon Yamamoto was introduced to motorsport at a very young age. At ten, reading a magazine article proved to be a turning point: he learned that starting racing after the age of twelve reduces the chances of reaching Formula 1 to less than 0.1 percent. For the child he was at the time, the conclusion was clear—time was running out. Without hesitation, he applied on his own initiative to the Suzuka Circuit Racing School.

The decision was not met with enthusiasm by his family. Motorsport is risky, uncertain, and expensive. Yet Yamamoto persisted—explaining, arguing, and insisting. Eventually, a compromise was reached: he would be allowed to try, under strict conditions. This marked the beginning of a demanding path, shaped early on by discipline and determination.

At the time, his role model was Ayrton Senna. The Brazilian driver embodied absolute excellence in his eyes. Senna’s sudden death in 1994 came as a shock, but it also triggered a profound shift in how Yamamoto viewed his own journey. No longer was the goal to resemble someone else, but rather to confront himself. Shortly thereafter, a sentence written on a New Year’s card from a senior driver left a lasting impression:

“We never imagine a dream that we are unable to achieve.”

This maxim would accompany him throughout his career.

It was in this context that the idea of political engagement emerged. Elected to the House of Representatives, he drew on his international experience, particularly in diplomacy, negotiation, and innovation‑related policy. He became especially involved in complex issues such as synthetic fuels, convinced that the energy transition could build on Japan’s industrial strengths.

Here again, the method remained the same: explain, persuade, bring people together—without giving up in the face of initial misunderstanding. The perseverance developed in Formula 1 found new resonance in the political arena.

# Itinéraires singuliers podcast - From the trading floor to sake breweries: Sébastien Lemoine’s rediscovered sense of purpose

Leaving a well-established career in international finance to turn to Japanese sake may seem like a radical shift. For Sébastien Lemoine, it is above all the culmination of a quest: finding meaning again. That is the word he chooses to sum up his journey. After years on trading floors, in a demanding environment sometimes dominated by greed and performance, he realizes his energy is gradually fading. The shock of the global financial crisis, followed by the Tohoku disaster in 2011, accelerates his reflection.

Japan is a country he has known for a long time. He first came in 1986 as a student, drawn by the language and the culture. He then returned regularly, eventually settling there for extended periods. He has seen the country evolve, age, and change pace. What was once a very young, vibrant Japan - onsen full of children, overflowing energy in Roppongi - has given way to an older society. Yet his attachment has only grown stronger. He walks, cycles, crosses countryside and cities, and finds in this close relationship with the country a form of obviousness, almost a feeling of being “where he belongs”.

It was from 2008 that he truly discovered Japanese sake. Not generic sake, but carefully crafted bottles rooted in a culture of long-term commitment. Japanese craftsmanship, he says, is not just a profession but a path. One strives for a perfection that is never fully reached, but approached by integrating each year’s experience, variations in climate, rice, and microorganisms. He cites the Kenbishi brewery in Kobe, which claims continuity across centuries and blends each year sakes drawn from a fifty-year stock to maintain a consistent taste profile despite natural changes.

# Itinéraires singuliers podcast - From the trading floor to sake breweries: Sébastien Lemoine’s rediscovered sense of purpose

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/itineraires-singuliers-de-la-salle-des-marches-aux-maisons-de-sake-le-sens-retrouve-de-sebastien-lemoine-1.html
In a context where sake consumption has fallen by fourfold in fifty years and many breweries struggle to find successors, Sébastien chooses a different role: neither producer nor trader, but a transmitter. He creates Passerelle, a company whose name reflects its mission: building a bridge between Japanese producers and international audiences. He teaches at Le Cordon Bleu and Temple University, guides enthusiasts, and introduces this world through education and tasting.

The welcome he receives in sake breweries surprises him. He expected more reserve. Instead, he encounters artisans proud of their heritage yet deeply humble, often facing economic difficulties. He recalls a visit in Chiba where a producer, to mark their exchange, opened for him and a friend a bottle from 1952, her year of birth. This generosity, he often finds, emerges when he shows genuine interest and a serious understanding of the product.

Nothing was instantaneous, however. In Japan, legitimacy comes through expertise. Moving from a field where one is an expert to another where one is not yet requires learning, understanding processes, categories, and practices. This in-depth work, combined with recommendations and the trust of certain producers, gradually opens the doors of the industry to him.

His contribution also lies in an external perspective. Where sake breweries often present their product from a technical angle - water, rice, know-how - he emphasizes the tasting experience and food pairings. Drawing on his French culture of food and wine pairing, he proposes new approaches: sake with Western cuisine, sake with cheese, sake served not merely as an accompaniment but as an element that directly interacts with the dish. He sees this as a way to renew interest in a declining market.

He finally recalls the cultural and symbolic dimension of sake, down to the objects that accompany it, such as the masu - the small wooden box once used to measure rice and from which sake is drunk during ceremonies or inaugurations. Simple gestures that tell part of Japan’s story.

# Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan

She could have stayed in Burgundy, at the heart of the Loiseau house, within the comfort of a well-established group.

But Blanche Loiseau chose to explore other avenues. In 2019, she went to Japan to work in a traditional kaiseki restaurant. A highly codified cuisine, devoid of foreigners and women. For a month, no one spoke to her. So she started washing dishes, observed, offered her help, and gradually earned her place. The sous-chef eventually took her under his wing. She emerged from that year with a rare glimpse into a Japan that is usually closed off. Daughter of a three-star chef and heir to a house whose name resonates throughout French gastronomy, she nonetheless describes a simple childhood in the family kitchen in Saulieu. A rabbit liver tartlet as her madeleine de Proust, a rule passed down by her father - never more than three main flavors on a plate - and a strong conviction: excellence can be pursued without brutality.

Today, she divides her time between France and Japan, working for Loiseau de France while overseeing teams and international openings.

This balance of gentleness and firmness also guides her management style. In Besançon, where she opened a restaurant in 2023, her team is mostly female. She sets a clear framework: if a customer crosses the line, she personally shows them the door, and will go as far as accompanying them to the police station if necessary. She wants demanding kitchens that are also safe, where young people - especially women - can work without being subjected to abuse.

# Itinéraires singuliers podcast - Blanche Loiseau, between heritage and boldness: a French chef in Japan

When the opportunity to open a restaurant in Tokyo arises in 2024, she accepts fully aware of what lies ahead. She discovers Japan’s inflexible administrative system, where even opening a bank account can take hours because her first names do not fit into predefined boxes. She also learns to work with very rigorous Japanese teams, sometimes lacking flexibility, but with rare reliability: once a gesture is set, it will be followed all year long.

In this context, she seeks a balance between French culture and Japanese codes. She demonstrates, corrects, and cleans the kitchen alongside her teams so they can leave earlier. Gradually, she earns their respect, without forcing it.

In her cuisine, Blanche finds natural bridges between Burgundy and the archipelago: the trilogy of flavors inherited from her father, purity of ingredients, and strict respect for the seasons. She appreciates the accepted imperfection of Japanese plating, inspired by kintsugi, where nothing is strictly identical yet everything makes sense. And when asked which dish to try in Tokyo, she recommends revisited œufs en meurette - before admitting that, for her, the true dish of Japan is ramen, which she could eat every day.

Her journey is that of a chef who carries a prestigious heritage without being confined by it. A French woman forging her own path between Saulieu and Tokyo, between tradition and movement, guided by a constant line: high standards, respect, and a certain idea of kindness in the kitchen.

# Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From Paris to Fukui: the odyssey of Virginie, a creator who brings together art and fashion in Japan

A French artist chooses the provinces over the fashion capitals and, through sheer perseverance, builds a brand that sells directly to Japan’s most discerning customers. Itinéraires Singuliers dedicates this episode to Virginie Lefèvre – founder of the brand Viruxiny – and to what her journey reveals about creative entrepreneurship in Japan.

Born to draw and paint, trained in fine arts and later in fashion, Virginie arrived in Japan 25 years ago to teach at Esmod. One year was supposed to be enough. But a profound aesthetic and human encounter rooted her on the archipelago. Marriage, motherhood, and an unexpected detour through Fukui – a discreet prefecture, yet an industrial giant in knitwear and techno-sozai materials. Where others might have seen a dead end, she saw an opportunity. She opened a small shop, met workshops supplying major luxury houses, learned the language, sales, and even sewing. From scratch.

Her vision of fashion is both simple and radical: to wear art. Each Viruxiny piece carries a positive message – love, protection of the sea and the earth, cultural blending – sometimes with a playful French touch, like a stylized Eiffel Tower. Against fast fashion and ultra fast fashion, she stands for creative honesty, proximity to her clients, and the long game. Little internet, a lot of fieldwork. She favors pop-up stores, listens to feedback, and refines her offer around two complementary axes: accessible pieces that create attachment and more intricate creations for true fashion lovers.

# Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From Paris to Fukui: the odyssey of Virginie, a creator who brings together art and fashion in Japan

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/itineraires-singuliers-podcast-from-paris-to-fukui-the-odyssey-of-virginie-a-creator-who-brings-together-art-and-fashion-in-japan.html
Behind the smiles and politeness, in Japan, business is business. Being a woman and a foreigner comes with its share of doubts and closed doors. So Virginie steps up to the front line. She sells herself, oversees her artistic direction, manages the numbers, speaks Japanese, and sets boundaries. They want her behind the cash register – she takes the cash register. She’s told that “in front of Japanese customers, it would be better to have Japanese staff” – she proves them wrong with results. A key anecdote: a group of artisans entrusted her with a mini collection, considered too risky with a designer not born in Fukui. She took it back and sold it out in a pop-up. More recently in Ginza, she achieved the highest clothing sales figures, outperforming established national brands. Respect earned on the ground.

Why Fukui instead of Tokyo or Paris? Because growing there means learning everything – from operating a sewing machine to drafting quotes, from local sourcing to understanding the codes of department stores. This school of reality built a solid network: loyal clients, department store directors, multiple agents (to stay independent), and allied entrepreneurs. And it shaped a conviction useful to anyone dreaming of setting up in Japan: rules of politeness must be respected, but a touch of kind audacity opens doors. Call, follow up, send a physical dossier when needed, show that you’re ready to work hard – and keep your promises.

On the practical side, the episode demystifies administration in Japan. You can start small as a sole proprietor, test your creations in local markets, handle your own accounting while volumes are modest, and bring in an accountant when things take off. Japanese language skills help, of course, but effort and reliability earn admiration. Japanese customers are demanding when it comes to quality and finishing – “they spot the tiny stitch that’s off” – and that’s a good thing: their standards clarify what excellence means, prevent shortcuts, and push you to do better.

# Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From Pharmacy to Distillation: How François Combes created Nagura, a Premium Rum born in Ishigaki

Itinéraires Singuliers dedicates this episode to François Combes – founder of Nagura – and to what his journey reveals about artisanal entrepreneurship in Japan, in the Okinawa archipelago where agricultural tradition meets innovation.

A trained pharmacist, François arrived in Japan in the 1990s for a product launch. He hadn’t planned to stay. Yet opportunity turned into belonging. His career took him through laboratories, distribution, pharmacy ownership, and finally real estate – always guided by the same instinct: spot the openings, step in, and learn by doing. Real estate eventually led him to Ishigaki , a gem of Okinawa – an agricultural and maritime island devoted to sugarcane, wagyu, and a fiercely protected rural way of life. Where others saw isolation, he saw an opportunity: after Japanese whisky and Japanese gin, why not a Japanese rum rooted in Ishigaki’s terroir?

His method is straightforward and deliberate: start, learn by doing, and solve one problem a day. Find farmland without being a farmer, convince the city hall and the prefecture, secure alcohol and agricultural licenses, import equipment, and prove sanitary compliance piece by piece. Build trust with local growers, listen before speaking, and earn acceptance. Rather than buying an existing operation, he built his own distillery. Two years later came the first production – and an unambiguous verdict: 'It’s good.'

Nagura proudly claims a Japanese identity. Locally selected typhoon-resistant sugarcane, hand-cut to prevent unwanted fermentations, pressed immediately, and distilled by a whisky-trained distiller for precision rather than effect. Nothing goes to waste: leaves and bagasse go back to farmers, vinasse becomes fertilizer. Minimal plastic, no boxes, Japanese labels. A small team of five to six people , including a local unit of workers with disabilities who handle pressing – a tangible way, as François puts it, to 'give back to the island.'

# Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From Pharmacy to Distillation: How François Combes created Nagura, a Premium Rum born in Ishigaki

When it comes to the market, François chose a short, dense funnel : first Ishigaki, then Miyako and Okinawa, followed by a few carefully selected addresses in Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka. The goal: a premium brand that grows through tasting, distillery visits, and bartender recommendations. The response? Connoisseurs speak of excellence, and the very first batch earned a gold medal in London. The aim isn’t to flood the internet, but to build a strong reputation among bars, hotels, and restaurants capable of telling the story behind the product.

The episode also breaks a few myths. Starting a company in Japan isn’t the hardest part. The real challenges lie with local banks that take their time, administrative licensing processes , and the strict rules of agricultural zoning . The key, according to François, isn’t waving a French business card as a golden ticket, but consistency : speaking Japanese, being on the ground, accepting early slowness, delivering on time, listening to feedback, and striving for operational perfection at every step – from harvesting to barrel aging, whether in bourbon casks, Japanese whisky barrels, or, more rarely, mizunara oak when it makes ecological sense.

The turning point came when Ishigaki’s bars began serving the rum. 'It’s their rum – the island’s rum,' says François. That local recognition changed everything: Nagura was no longer seen as a Frenchman’s project, but as an island’s pride , a product born from its soil and carried by its people. This sense of ownership became both a shield against failure – the island supports it – and a springboard to Tokyo , where authenticity rooted in place sparks curiosity.

What’s next? Strengthening roots in Okinawa, expanding carefully across Japan, and opening export windows once aged stock allows it. Always guided by the same credo: succeed first where you are. The episode becomes a how-to guide for building in Japan outside the megacities : choose a territory, enter humbly into its networks, respect local standards, and keep your product promise.

# Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - From translator to sports commentator: how Florent Dabadie built his place in Japan

Arriving in Japan in 1994, Florent Dabadie did not plan to work in sports. A literature lover, trained in Oriental languages, he discovered a country whose social framework matched his sensibilities: a highly codified attention to others, politeness viewed as the foundation of living together. Where many see constraint, he sees a structure that reassures and stimulates.

The turning point came almost by chance. Then a young editorial coordinator for Hachette in Tokyo, he responded to a job ad: the Japan Football Association was looking for an interpreter for a French coach. A rare profile, a unique opportunity. He suddenly found himself thrust into the heart of professional football: crowded press conferences, the discipline of the locker room, travels to the four corners of the world. A crash course not only in language, but in observing cultures.

This immersion revealed a paradox to him: on the international stage, Japanese players face a cultural shock as much as a sporting one. Domestic football remains sheltered, perhaps too much so. These athletes therefore need to be prepared for what awaits them beyond the national cocoon: intensity, confrontation, unpredictability.

Moving into sports journalism, first in football then in tennis, Florent observed that sport has become in Japan a vector for openness. The national team captures public attention far more than the domestic league. Organizers take great care in their hospitality, foreign athletes feel confident, journalists find it easier to engage in conversation than elsewhere. Top-level sport has become a showcase for the country to the world.

Yet everyday life does not come down to the hospitality extended to visitors. Integrating the codes takes time: hierarchy, rituals, caution in relationships. One must find room to maneuver without upsetting the balance. Florent speaks of adaptation, not renunciation: learning the rules in order to know when and how to deviate from them.

On the pitch as in the stands, another distinct feature remains: the atmosphere is passionate yet controlled. Supporters are committed, but helpful. Few disturbances. It is a family experience. A notable contrast with the image of football in Europe.

After 25 years in the field, his conclusion is pragmatic: curiosity is a method. It makes it possible to listen, to decode, to build bridges between two cultures that sometimes struggle to understand each other, especially in humor or direct expression. It also helps one remain oneself without becoming isolated.

Florent Dabadie did not choose Japan for its exoticism, but because he feels at ease there. By speaking about sport, he connects two worlds every day that are trying to understand each other better.

# Itinéraires Singuliers Podcast - In just one year in Tokyo, Gemmyo shines bright: Pauline Laigneau’s lessons on success

Opening a French fine jewelry house in Tokyo could seem like a daunting challenge. For Pauline Laigneau , founder of Gemmyo , it was instead the natural extension of a principle she has followed from the very beginning: independence of mind .

More than a motto, it’s her way of life. Not acting to please, but acting with integrity. This compass led her far from the academic path set by her education at the prestigious École Normale Supérieure. Instead of an intellectual career, she chose entrepreneurship — sparked by an aesthetic revelation before an engagement ring: wearable sculptures, stones millions of years old, symbols meant to be passed on. She saw a magnificent but frozen world, where warmth was missing. Gemmyo was born from the desire to put colored gemstones back at the center , combining precision, sincerity, and accessibility.

Why Tokyo rather than elsewhere in Asia? Because, according to Pauline, Japanese clients share the same taste as Parisians : discretion, refinement, and meaning. No loud logos — just “intentional jewelry.” Japan became a bold, intuitive move, without endless market studies. Omotesando felt like the natural twin of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: broad streets, art galleries, quiet elegance. The boutique brings Parisian codes (herringbone parquet floors) into subtle dialogue with local ones (stone ceilings, sliding screens for privacy). The construction even finished ahead of schedule — a rarity — and from day one, customers understood the balance: French spirit, Japanese precision .

A clear lesson soon emerged: what works in France works in Japan. Each time the team over-adapted, it backfired — smaller ring sizes, the wrong inventory, flashy influencer campaigns that didn’t resonate. The turnaround came by returning to Gemmyo’s fundamentals: intimate events with real clients, honest storytelling, made-to-order craftsmanship in France, and personal meaning expressed through each gemstone. In the showroom, they don’t sell objects; they adjust symbols .

The Tokyo team of three Japanese advisors — led by Erika-san — maintains a daily link with Paris through WhatsApp and Slack, even joining company seminars in France. Service follows Japanese etiquette, but adds a distinctly Gemmyo touch: genuine advice, even the courage to say no when a piece doesn’t suit. That frankness, rare in Japan, builds trust. And while Japanese preparation is meticulous to the extreme, management strives to focus that precision on what truly matters.

The results speak for themselves. In its first year, the Tokyo boutique generated around €2 million in sales , with the feeling that growth is just beginning. And sometimes, the best way to adapt to Japan is not to over-adapt.

# Itinéraires singuliers – Yuji Hirayama :World climbing champion looks back on his journey, his passion for climbing and his strong connection with France

He could have continued his journey in Japan. Yet at 19, Yuji Hirayama set off for France with one goal in mind: to discover how Europe’s best climbers trained and to reach the very highest level of the sport himself.

This experience would profoundly transform not only his approach to climbing, but also his outlook on the world. After spending several years in France, he returned to Japan and became one of the most iconic climbers of his generation. More than 40 years after he first started climbing, he continues to pursue the sport while sharing his experience through his climbing gyms and various projects dedicated to the discipline.

“The environment is important. I wanted to go to Europe to learn how to climb at the highest level and bring that experience back to Japan.”

## Setting Off for France

Yuji Hirayama discovered climbing at the age of 15 and quickly set himself the goal of competing with the best climbers in the world. After his first trip to the United States at 17, he became particularly interested in the European climbing scene and the training methods he encountered, notably through French climbing magazines.

At 19, he decided to move to France with several friends. After arriving in Marseille, he settled in the Luberon region. He spoke very little French and found himself in a country whose customs and culture were still largely unfamiliar to him.

Beyond climbing, the experience quickly became a genuine cultural immersion. He learned the language, discovered a different way of life and became familiar with another approach to sport. He was particularly struck by the more structured preparation of French climbers, for whom training and recovery each played an important role.

Above all, this period allowed him to take a step back and reassess his own climbing. Balancing the discipline of European training with a certain freedom in the way he approached the sport, Yuji Hirayama gradually developed his own philosophy of climbing.

## From the Summit to Years of Doubt

## From the Summit to Years of Doubt

The results soon followed. Hirayama reached the highest levels of international climbing and took on some of the hardest routes of his time. Yet behind his performances, a more personal question gradually emerged: why keep climbing once the goals he had set himself as a teenager had been achieved?

For several years, training and competition became a routine. The pursuit of performance no longer always provided a sense of purpose.

Another trip to the United States, at the age of 25, marked a turning point. His perspective on the world began to change. He started looking at the shapes, materials and objects around him with a newfound curiosity. He came to understand that all those years devoted to climbing had also shaped the way he thought and perceived his surroundings.

“Not giving up really mattered. Even when you can’t immediately find the answer, you can keep moving forward and take the time to look for it.”

This realisation gradually helped him rediscover a more peaceful relationship with climbing. It was no longer just about results, but also a way to explore, learn and continue to grow.

## Sharing Climbing Beyond Competition

After dedicating much of his life to competition and elite-level climbing, Yuji Hirayama also decided to create spaces where others could discover and practise the sport.

He founded Base Camp, a network of climbing gyms primarily located in the Tokyo and Saitama regions. What was initially intended as a personal training space gradually became a place open to a wide range of people: children, elite athletes and older climbers simply looking to stay active and healthy.

Today, his commitment extends beyond the climbing gyms themselves. Based in a region close to the mountains of Saitama, he also takes part in projects aimed at revitalising local communities through climbing, promoting natural climbing areas and building connections between climbers, visitors and residents.

His journey between France and Japan naturally informs this desire to build bridges. Having spent several years in Europe, he explains that he also came to rediscover his own country and certain aspects of his Japanese identity.

This week, Japan’s central bank raised interest rates for the first time in 17 years. Still, rates are remaining close to zero, opening a symbolic bre

After years of deflation with little change in prices, wages and cost of money, Japanese people are assessing how to adapt to higher borrowing costs.

Japanese companies and households have been content to play the deflationary game , hoarding cash and cutting costs. # Japan Experience joins the Havas Voyages Group and accelerates its growth

Japan Experience announced in late December 2025 that it had been acquired 100 percent by the Havas Voyages group (Marietton Développement), the leading tourism player in France.

Founded in 1981, Japan Experience has established itself over the years as a reference player for travel to Japan, with a unique positioning covering the entire value chain - travel agency, tour operator, and destination management company. The company employed nearly 100 staff across Europe (Paris, Milan, Madrid, Berlin, London) and Japan (Tokyo, Kyoto). Each year, around 300,000 travelers benefited from its services. In 2025, the company generated revenue of 70 million euros and had been profitable continuously since its creation.

This partnership with Havas Voyages formed part of a strategy focused on growth and complementarity. The Marietton Développement group aimed to strengthen its expertise in Japan, a rapidly expanding destination, while leveraging Japan Experience’s well-recognized digital know-how. In 2024, Japan welcomed 37 million international visitors, including 400,000 French travelers, and the Japanese authorities were targeting 60 million foreign visitors by 2030.

The transaction enabled Japan Experience to rely on Havas Voyages’ international network and distribution strength, while maintaining its specialist positioning and digital DNA. The stated objective was to double the size of the company within five years, particularly through international expansion and B2B development.

“Joining Havas Voyages means offering Japan Experience a strong and visionary partner to accelerate our development, while preserving what makes us strong - our passion for Japan, the expertise of our teams, and digital innovation in the service of our clients,” said Thierry Maincent, CEO of Japan Experience.

# Japanese cybersecurity recruitment on the rise

Facing the threat of cyber-attacks, more and more Japanese companies are recruiting in the field of cybersecurity.

A “ red ocean in a red ocean ”, according to Recruit (a Japanese company specializing in human resources). Competition for cybersecurity talent is fierce in Japan. According to a Recruit study published this month, the number of cybersecurity-related jobs was 24.3 times higher in 2023 than in 2002.

The years 2018 - 2019 saw a particular increase linked to the growing concern about cyber attack risks during the Tokyo Olympics, which were due to take place in 2020.

The rise in demand for jobs since 2020 can be explained by the pandemic. A number of cyber-attacks have targeted the shift to teleworking, leaving corporate VPNs vulnerable. Faced with such risks, some companies have been forced to suspend operations.

Although the number of opportunities is increasing, few people have actually changed jobs. Recruit states “[that] it is difficult to recruit people with immediate skills, unless you can offer them attractive annual salaries in line with market conditions.”

Faced with this recruitment difficulty, companies are forced to review their recruitment strategy, in particular by offering in-house training courses. In some cases, companies are calling on IT specialists even if they have no practical experience in cybersecurity.

# Japanese land prices rise for the third year running

Land prices in Japan have risen by 3% for the first time since the speculative bubble.

Announced on March 26 by the Ministry of Land and Transport (Kokudo-kotsu-sho), Japanese land prices rose by 2.4% year-on-year . This is the third consecutive year of increases, and the highest rate of growth since the speculative bubble.

Indeed, after the bubble burst, land prices in Japan remained negative for a long time. However, the rise in land prices marks a turning point in Japan’s deflationary recovery, going hand in hand with rising equities and wages. The question is whether this momentum can be maintained in the future, while stimulating the economy at the same time.

In addition to strong housing demand in the main metropolitan areas (Tokyo, Osaka and Nagoya) and the four regional cities (Sapporo, Sendai, Hiroshima and Fukuoka), rural areas are also affected .

In Tokyo, the return of office work has led to a reduction in telecommuting, with commercial land rising by an average of 7.0%. According to Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation, vacancy rates around JR Yamanote stations remain at around 3%.

For the eighteenth year running, the highest price was 55.7 million yen (approximately $370,000) per square meter in Ginza, Tokyo.

# Jean Todt Presents the Global “Make A Safety Statement” Campaign at CCI France Japon

On September 16, 2025, the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCI France Japon) had the honor of welcoming Jean Todt , United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Envoy for Road Safety, for a CEO Breakfast Conference held in Tokyo.

A former iconic leader of the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) , Jean Todt now works alongside the United Nations to raise awareness among the public and policymakers on a global issue: road safety . Every year, road accidents cause nearly 1.3 million deaths worldwide.

A Global Campaign in Partnership with JCDecaux

During his presentation at CCI France Japon, Jean Todt introduced the new global campaign #MakeASafetyStatement , launched by the United Nations in partnership with JCDecaux .

The campaign was unveiled on September 12 at Expo 2025 Osaka , alongside Japanese Olympic skateboarding champion Cocona Hiraki , before being displayed at the United Nations Pavilion (September 12-15) . It is also being rolled out across 10 cities and airports in Japan : Fukuoka, Hiroshima, Kawasaki, Kobe, Sendai, Nagoya, Osaka, Sapporo, Tokyo, and Yokohama.

The goal is clear: to engage citizens on the importance of simple, responsible actions while driving, riding a motorcycle or bicycle, or walking, and to remind everyone that each of us can contribute to saving lives .

Renowned Ambassadors

The campaign features internationally recognized faces to amplify this universal message. Among them is Academy Award-winning actress Michelle Yeoh , also Jean Todt’s spouse, who lends her image to the initiative to enhance its impact with the public.

## An Exclusive Interview with Jean Todt

Following the conference, CCI France Japon had the privilege of conducting an exclusive interview with Jean Todt , together with Régis Arnaud , editor-in-chief of France Japon Eco and journalist at Le Figaro .

# Joint Statement on the Entry Restrictions in Japan

On November 12, the CCI France Japon, together with the American, British, Canadian, German and Italian Chambers of Commerce in Japan and the European European Business Council, issued a joint statement on the entry restrictions in Japan.

The American Chamber of Commerce in Japan (ACCJ), British Chamber of Commerce in Japan (BCCJ), Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Japan (CCCJ), German Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (AHK Japan), French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCI France Japon), Italian Chamber, and the European Business Council in Japan (EBC), welcome the change to the Government of Japan’s inbound travel policy that took effect on November 8, 2021. Permitting business travelers and students to once again enter Japan is a critical step toward Japan’s post-COVID-19 economic recovery. It will help to ensure that international businesses operating in Japan can continue serving their clients and customers in country and is a necessary precondition to attracting new investment and talent from overseas to meet Japan’s economic goals.

We also welcome the reduction from 10 to three days for the quarantine period required of vaccinated business travelers permitted to enter Japan as well as the proposed new measure to allow pre-approved movements after the third day.

However, we note with concern that even with the aforementioned changes, new reporting requirements imposed on sponsoring companies and organizations, as well as other regulatory requirements, mean that Japan will remain more difficult to enter than most of its major economic partners, including other G7 countries.

Further, the continuing requirement for business travelers to obtain a visa (up to 3 months’ stay) leads to a significant increase in administrative burden for Japanese and international companies, while limits on the number of businesspeople entering the country adds further uncertainty and complications.

In light of the aforementioned issues and recognizing that the safe resumption of international travel is vital to Japan’s economy, we request:

# Joint Statement on the Entry Restrictions in Japan

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/joint-statement-on-the-entry-restrictions-in-japan.html
In light of the aforementioned issues and recognizing that the safe resumption of international travel is vital to Japan’s economy, we request:

● Simplification of, and greater transparency for, the decision-making process for obtaining visas for business travelers. ● The Government of Japan to move as rapidly as possible to eliminate quarantines and to simplify and eventually eliminate sponsorship procedures for vaccinated travelers. ● The Government of Japan to consider increasing the limits on the number of business people entering the country in the near future. We have appreciated the Government of Japan’s efforts to limit the spread of COVID-19 in Japan and to accelerate vaccination of the population, including all foreign residents.

Further, we applaud the Japanese government’s willingness to recognize digital vaccination systems implemented in many major partner countries, such as the SMART system used widely in the United States and across Europe. ● To further facilitate the smooth resumption of international travel, we request that Japan enhance its procedures by recognizing the validity of all vaccines accredited by the World Health Organization for entry into Japan. We commend the Government of Japan for re-opening its borders to international students. International education is critically important as an industry itself and more broadly as a vital incubator of the talent on which business depends. Unfortunately, the new procedures required of students seeking to study in Japan are costly, time-consuming, and onerous. These procedures and the resulting delays constitute a barrier to international education and will deter, rather than facilitate, international students from studying in Japan. ● In this context, we strongly encourage the Government of Japan to take immediate steps to simplify, expedite, and lower costs for entry of students into Japan. Finally, we request that the entry process at Japan’s airports, which can currently take many hours, be streamlined. Fuller utilization of digital documentation could substantially reduce entry waiting times, reduce costs, and help prepare for eventual expansion of visitor numbers as public health conditions permit. We look forward to having the opportunity to discuss these recommendations, and to continuing to support Japan’s economic recovery and growth.

On June 30, as part of the Osaka World Expo , the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCI France Japon) had the pleasure of hosting a networking event between a delegation of 30 Monegasque companies led by the Monaco Economic Board (MEB) and a selection of Japanese companies.

The event was initially held at the Australian Pavilion due to space availability and began at 11:00 AM with an inspiring and insightful talk by Mr. Jiri Mestecky , Registered Foreign Attorney at Kitahama Partners, a member of the Chamber. Mr. Mestecky highlighted the economic vitality and attractiveness of the Kansai region: a hub of Japanese industry, strategically located at the center backbone, extremely well-connected to the rest of Japan and the world through two major ports and three airports. He emphasized the region's highly skilled and well-educated workforce, thanks to its rich academic ecosystem, combined with significantly lower wage costs and a cost of living that is 15% lower than in the capital. Mr. Mestecky also pointed out the region’s unparalleled cultural appeal, as it represents the historical heart of Japan.

This made for a perfect introduction for the companies from the Principality of Monaco seeking to expand their activities in Japan.

Jean-François Rauch, Regional Director of CCI France Japon, then introduced the Chamber’s mission and activities in the region. This was followed by a joint presentation from MEB representatives Guillaume Rose (CEO) and Justin Highman (Deputy CEO), who highlighted Monaco’s strengths as a destination for international business development and investment. A roundtable session allowed each Monegasque company to briefly introduce itself, paving the way for targeted and meaningful networking opportunities.

At 12:30 PM, the exchanges continued in a friendly atmosphere over a networking cocktail held at the Monaco Pavilion, in the presence of distinguished guests, including:

# Le chômage partiel comme réponse sociale au CORONAVIRUS

Cet article est fourni gracieusement par Davy Le Doussal, avocat au Barreau de Paris enregistré au Barreau de Tokyo et son confrère Seiji Kurihara, associé du cabinet TMI Associates, membre bienfaiteur de la CCI France Japon.

Si la situation sanitaire engendrée par le COVID-19 donne l’apparence d’être contenue au Japon, un certain nombre d’entreprises n’en est pas moins confronté à de sérieuses difficultés résultant de problèmes dans les chaines d’approvisionnement, de chute de fréquentation ou plus généralement de trésorerie. Tout comme ANA qui a annoncé mettre 5.000 de ses employés en chômage partiel (1) , il est plus que probable que les filiales de groupes français présents au Japon et les entrepreneurs établis dans l’archipel devront recourir à de semblables mesures pour préserver l’emploi dans l’attente de la reprise. Nous vous proposons donc ci-dessous un rappel des grandes lignes applicable au chômage partiel au Japon.

## 1. La suspension des contrats de travail pour motif économique

Confrontés à des difficultés économiques, les employeurs ont, comme en France, la possibilité de suspendre les contrats de leurs salariés sous réserve de conclure un accord collectif d’ajustement de l’emploi (1.1.). Mais cette suspension des contrats de travail n’exonère pas les employeurs de toute obligation vis-à-vis des salariés dont les contrats ont été suspendus : ils doivent en effet leur verser une indemnité de suspension de contrat (kyûgyôteate ou 休業手当 en japonais) (1.2).

1.1. La conclusion d’un accord d’ajustement de l’emploi

1.1. La conclusion d’un accord d’ajustement de l’emploi

Pour mettre en place une activité partielle au sein de leur établissement, les employeurs doivent conclure par écrit et avant toute mise en oeuvre un accord collectif (rôshikyotei ou 労使協定 en japonais)avec un syndicat représentant plus de la moitié des salariés ou, à defaut, un représentant de plus de la moitié des salariés.

Cet accord doit au minimum préciser la durée prévisionnelle du recours à l’activité partielle (2) , son nombre de jours, le nombre d’heures concernées, les catégories et le nombre de salariés concernés et les modalités de calcul de l’indemnité de suspension de contrat versée par l’employeur.

1.2. Le versement d’une indemnité de suspension de contrat

Quand bien même leurs contrats de travail sont suspendus, les employeurs n’en sont pas moins tenus de verser aux salariés concernés une indemnité de suspension de contrat partielle dont le montant doit au minimum correspondre à 60% du salaire moyen versé au cours des trois derniers mois. Des dispositions contractuelles ou conventionnelles peuvent parfois prévoir un pourcentage plus élevé.

Aux termes de l’article 26 de la loi sur les conditions de travail, le versement d’une telle indemnité incombe à l’employeur dès lors que la raison de la suspension du contrat de travail lui est imputable, ce qui est généralement considéré être le cas lorsque la suspension des contrats de travail provient de difficultés économiques affectant l’employeur.

L’agence pour l’emploi peut être amenée à verser une subvention aux entreprises qui en font la demande. Les conditions générales de versement de cette subvention sont assez strictes (2.1), mais il a été décidé par les autorités publiques japonaises de les assouplir pour préserver la situation de l’emploi dans le contexte de la crise sanitaire (2.2).

2.1. Des conditions ordinaires strictes d’application

2.1. Des conditions ordinaires strictes d’application

Les employeurs qui font face à des difficultés économiques suite notamment à des modifications de l’environnement économique ou des mutations de la structure industrielle et qui sont amenés à réduire leur activité et par voie de conséquence à mettre en place un plan d’activité partielle peuvent déposer une demande de subvention auprès de l’agence pour l’emploi dont ils dépendent. Le montant de cette subvention couvre les 2/3 pour les PME ou la moitié dans les grandes sociétés de l’indemnité de suspension de contrat versée aux salariés concernés, et ce dans la limite d’un plafond journalier par salarié. Des conditions de production et d’emploi très strictes doivent être remplies par les entreprises qui sollicitent cette subvention (4) .

Cette subvention n’est accordée que pour une certaine durée et ne peut être sollicitée de nouveau avant l’expiration d’un intervalle d’un an.

Lors de l’examen de la demande de subvention, l’agence de l’emploi s’assure de la réalité des conditions de difficultés économiques et de réduction de l’activité qui justifient son versement.

2.2. L’assouplissement exceptionnel des conditions d’éligibilité

Afin d’aider les entreprises maintenir l’emploi, les pouvoirs publics japonais ont annoncé des mesures d’assouplissement des conditions de versement des subventions d’ajustement de l’emploi.

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/le-japon-a-la-conquete-de-la-france-et-de-leurope-votre-propriete-intellectuelle-suit-elle-ce-rythme.html
