# Japan’s Expansion into France and Europe: Is your Intellectual Property keeping pace?

€45 billion: this is the amount of SoftBank’s investments announced at the Choose France 2026 Summit, making Japan the leading Asian investor in France.

This figure is no coincidence: nearly 490 subsidiaries of Japanese companies are currently established in France, employing approximately 74,000 people. Toyota, for example, has invested more than €1.5 billion in its plant in the Hauts-de-France region and, since 2022, has become the country’s leading car manufacturer.

Murata, for its part, has made its Caen site — acquired through the takeover of French start-up IPDia — one of its main operations in Europe, investing €60 million in its expansion.

And the economic opportunities extend well beyond France’s borders. France is a strategic gateway to the European Single Market, its 27 Member States and 450 million consumers. In this context, market entry must be strategically planned from the outset, particularly when it comes to protecting intangible assets.

Are your innovations and know-how as well protected in Europe as the capital you invest there?

Japan currently ranks third worldwide in terms of patent filings, with more than 419,000 applications filed in 2024. This exceptional capacity for innovation represents a considerable economic asset when entering the European market — provided, however, that these innovations are also protected in Europe.

A trademark protected only in Japan, a patent that has not been extended to Europe, or know-how shared without a solid contractual framework when establishing a subsidiary: these are all vulnerabilities that can prove costly for a company, whether it is a major industrial group or an SME expanding into Europe.

Contrary to a common misconception, securing intellectual property rights in Europe is not reserved for large corporations. Protection costs can be optimised by filing applications with the EUIPO for trademarks and designs and/or the EPO for patents, making it possible to secure protection across multiple European markets through centralised procedures.

# Japan’s Expansion into France and Europe: Is your Intellectual Property keeping pace?

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/le-japon-a-la-conquete-de-la-france-et-de-leurope-votre-propriete-intellectuelle-suit-elle-ce-rythme.html
However, proceeding without the support of a French Patent & Trademark Attorney (Conseil en propriété industrielle – CPI) would be unwise. As a recognised intellectual property expert, a CPI is a key partner for companies seeking to secure their innovations in Europe.

The French Patent & Trademark Attorney: your partner in securing your IP in Europe

A French Patent & Trademark Attorney (CPI) is an independent professional specialising in advice and strategic assistance in intellectual property matters, both in France and across Europe.

The profession includes engineers, scientists and lawyers who have undergone rigorous professional training and qualification. Their core role is to guide companies in the protection, defence, and promotion of their intellectual property rights , including trademarks, patents, designs, software and know-how.

In practical terms, a French Patent & Trademark Attorney can assist you in three essential areas:

- Strategy and filing: defining the best approach to protecting and promoting your intangible assets, even before establishing your business in Europe;

- Contracts and disputes: drafting assignment or licensing agreements, preventing disputes and advising you in cases of infringement;

- Optimisation and value creation: auditing and assessing your intellectual property, particularly in connection with growth transactions or fundraising.

All CPIs, or French Patent & Trademark Attorneys , are members of the CNCPI (Compagnie Nationale des Conseils en Propriété Industrielle) , the only legally established organisation representing all French Patent & Trademark Attorneys.

The profession was created under French law in 1990. French Patent & Trademark Attorneys provide companies with specialised expertise in the protection, defence and promotion of their intellectual property rights.

Working with a French Patent & Trademark Attorney therefore means being advised by a qualified professional bound by professional obligations and with in-depth knowledge of the French and European intellectual property systems.

Franco-Japanese cooperation already in action

Close ties between France and Japan in the field of intellectual property are nothing new. For several years, the CNCPI has maintained strong relationships with the JPAA (Japan Patent Attorneys Association) and the JIPA (Japan Intellectual Property Association) .

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/le-japon-a-la-conquete-de-la-france-et-de-leurope-votre-propriete-intellectuelle-suit-elle-ce-rythme.html
More recently, another important step was taken. In 2025, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed between the CNCPI and the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan (CCI France Japon) , focusing on economic cooperation, innovation and industrial property.

The CCIFJ organized a week-long Learning Expedition for students of ESCP Business School’s Executive Master in Managing Projects and Transformation.

The French Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Japan developed an immersive program for a cohort of students from ESCP’s Executive Master in Managing Projects and Transformation. Scheduled at the end of their program, this journey offered participants a unique opportunity to explore Japan’s business ecosystem through direct engagement with leading corporations, institutions, and innovators.

Structured as an intensive, week-long experience, the Learning Expedition combined strategic insights, on-site visits, and high-level discussions, showcasing how Japan effectively integrates innovation, digital transformation, and operational excellence across diverse sectors.

Day 1 – Foundations: Economic Outlook, Business Culture, and Transformation

This foundational session set the tone for the week, emphasizing the importance of understanding Japan not merely as a market but as a complex ecosystem shaped by culture, long-term vision, and continuous improvement.

In the afternoon, the group visited Exotec , a French logistics robotics company that rapidly expanded in the Japanese market after forming a partnership with retail giant Uniqlo, which now uses Exotec robots in its warehouses. Participants met with Pierre Perdiguier, Exotec’s Vice President for Japan, and explored how a high-growth technology company successfully entered and scaled in Japan by meeting the country’s exacting standards for quality, reliability, and performance. The visit highlighted the strategic importance of partnerships, particularly with major Japanese clients, in supporting international expansion.

# Advice from an importer of agri food products in Japan

A specialist in the import of French agri food products in Japan answers our questions

On June 21, 2023, we had the pleasure of interviewing Mr. François Xavier COLAS, Managing Director of the Japanese branch of Classic Fine Foods , known as French F&B Japan , a company importing high end agri food products, present in Japan for 40 years.

80% of the products imported by Classic Fine Foods Japan are European, of which 70% are French. The company imports and distributes high quality ingredients dedicated to cooking and pastry, as well as dry grocery products. Its clients are luxury hotels, fine dining restaurants, reception venues, airline caterers, as well as wholesalers supplying pastry shops.

### Discover the advice of an expert on developing on the Japanese market and certain practices of importers.

His analysis of distribution channels in Japan :

In Japan, agri food products can be distributed through several types of stores, each playing a different role and corresponding to a different strategy:

- Department stores make it possible to enhance the image of the brand and the product and to sell at higher prices, however the volumes purchased are limited. Department stores only pay for what they have sold and return the rest to the importer. Indeed, using an importer is essential to work with department stores, as responsibilities are borne by the importer. In particular, the importer is responsible for providing a salesperson.

- High end supermarkets such as Seijo Ishii, Kaldi, Kinokuniya, Meidi ya, Meidi ya, Nissin, National Azabu are importer distributors. They import directly and allow larger volumes to be sold and better margins compared to department stores. They pay for everything they purchase and take the risk of stocking the goods. Within this channel, products are renewed every three years to meet customers’ expectations for novelty.

# Advice from an importer of agri food products in Japan

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/les-conseils-dun-importateur-de-produits-agroalimentaires-au-japon.html
- Finally, large supermarkets and convenience stores (Japanese convenience shops open 24/7) are the ones that purchase the largest volumes from foreign exporters. They are managed by Japanese trading houses such as Mitsui Bussan, Mitsubishi, which act as importers and distributors. These contracts are very significant and more difficult to obtain.

These three channels are organized like a pyramid, from top to bottom, from department stores to supermarkets and convenience stores.

Sales volumes will be lower at the department store level but the product will gain visibility, while supermarkets and convenience stores can allow large volumes to be sold but do not build the brand image of the product.

It is possible to change distribution channels in order to evolve one’s strategy, however this can only be done from top to bottom .

For example, the brand La Mère Poulard gained its reputation in department stores and was later able to develop its sales through other distribution channels.

How do importers work ?

A local importer will be your key and indispensable partner to develop on the Japanese market. Importers of agri food products handle product registration with customs, shipment to Japan, and the storage of your goods in their dedicated warehouses before distributing them.

Japanese importers favor exclusive contracts . If this is essential for your Japanese partner, try to associate them with performance related objectives (turnover communication, points of sale, development strategy, marketing tools, etc.) which will help foster a transparent relationship.

For example, Classic Fine Foods sends commercial reports every three months detailing the evolution of its overall turnover and the revenue generated by different products, product by product performance, as well as distribution locations.

His advice on best practices to adopt :

To export to Japan, product quality alone is not sufficient; it is also necessary to be flexible regarding packaging, conditioning, and the quantities per package (stricter weight constraints and different eating habits in Japan).

# Advice from an importer of agri food products in Japan

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/les-conseils-dun-importateur-de-produits-agroalimentaires-au-japon.html
To export to Japan, product quality alone is not sufficient; it is also necessary to be flexible regarding packaging, conditioning, and the quantities per package (stricter weight constraints and different eating habits in Japan).

It is advisable to come to Japan to understand the market, to test the potential of one’s product in order to determine whether it is sufficiently adapted, and to identify what interests local consumers the most. When you are a small company, one of the best ways to enter the Japanese market is to participate in trade shows in order to present your products to potential partners and consumers.

On the other hand, Japanese companies do not favor direct calls from foreign companies. Being introduced through a local intermediary is a good way to establish initial contact. There are various consulting organizations. CCI France Japan, thanks to its 100 years of presence in the country, has acquired a certain reputation that allows it to open doors for French companies.

To support the work of an importing partner, it is beneficial to have a local representative who masters the language and Japanese business culture . This person can support the importer in its commercial strategy in order to find new clients. It is important to note that Japanese people do not primarily have a sales driven mindset; they above all have a strong sense of service . Relationships with existing distributors and logistics are very well managed, but promotion and sales may require external support. According to Mr. Colas: “ delegation without control is abandonment ”.

To conclude, once distributed in Japan, it is essential to keep in mind that product quality must remain flawless ; otherwise, it could mean the end of exports to Japan.

Regulations to keep in mind :

In the agri food sector, the most sensitive products to export are fresh products. Large scale retailers only accept products when more than 50% of their use by date remains . It is therefore necessary to take this rule into account, as well as shipping time (46 days by sea from Europe, for example) and customs clearance (2 weeks).

Mascarpone, for example, is difficult to import due to its 150 day shelf life.

# Digital Transformation: Time Saving

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/looking-back-at-the-2nd-kansai-sectoral-meeting-digital-transformation-by-marion-baillat.html
Here we are, inaugurating the second episode of our Kansai Sectoral Gatherings, 2023. Our guest speaker this time is Marion Baillat, head of production at 42 Interactive , and her specialty is time saving through digital transformation . As she brilliantly demonstrated through a practical case (to manage a complex real estate), digital transformation is a long and complex but crucial and worthy process , which helps businesses make the transition from an heterogeneous analog system to an organized and efficient digital system . Efficiency is the key, but because the digital transformation fundamentally changes the way a business operates to deliver a higher value of service, one of the key issues that was debated during the speech was onboarding : if you want the change to take roots, there is a necessity that everybody in the company (and its partners) feels involved in the change and takes it up willingly. Thus, there is not only a technical issue , but there is also a really deep people issue . In fact, the process of digital transformation requires a deep understanding of the structure’s functioning, which is a challenge in itself. For the digital transformation to be relevant and involve the people it will benefit on the ground, there is a critical need to put yourself in their shoes and deeply understand what is at stake in what they do to make their life easier and simpler . If the solution is just forced from above, failure is nearly certain. The bottom line is, digital transformation is a patient and painstaking work that requires a lot of consideration. Wherever it takes place, it will not happen overnight, let alone be dropped brutally on a given organization. But if it is such a delicate process, how to make the need for digital transformation be felt, when it is so easy to leave things be and stay in your comfort zone? Efficiency is the key. The amount of money and time saved through a streamlined digital workflow , as opposed to paper processing, can save 4 times the time , and the cost of it in money can amount to millions of dollars for big structures. Teamwork and the employee’s quality of life are also strongly impacted, as well as security and internal access to information/documentation, while the quality of the service delivered to customers is increased.

# Crêpe party in Kansai!

Candlemas is originally a religious holiday, but nowadays it is mostly the occasion to eat crêpes and... make new acquaintances!

Being a crêpe enthusiast, it would have been a shame to miss such an opportunity to make and eat some!

Considering how fast our 10 guests made the hundred crêpes ? prepared by yours truly disappear, they shared that belief. This dinner, which was meant to be relaxed and informal, was originally intended to animate our Osaka Business Center . Our goal is indeed to increase conviviality between all the representatives of our resident companies, which are renting the office space provided by the CCIFJ inside our walls.

Our friends from Air France KLM did answer the call, but they were not alone to join us. Eventually many distinguished guests surrendered to the crêpes' perfume and came to Avanza to sit around the meeting table with us. The conference room had been turned into a dining room of sort for the occasion. Honey, chocolate, sugar, jam, ham & eggs: there was something for every taste. A few bottles, some of them graciously offered by Morikawa Clinic from Kobe, helped loosen the tongues and warm the atmosphere.

Mr. Seiichirō Hayashi , our Ambassador of the Chamber in Kyoto and undisputed life of the party, amused everybody with his witticism, which would belong in a French salon. Always kind and quick, he offered that everyone attending the party would say a few words before leaving, so as to alleviate the melancholy of ending the evening. A news, an announcement, anything that would be worth sharing with the assistance. Everybody complied, and not only did it allow us to know each other better, but it also gave everyone a good chance to give some information regarding an upcoming event, a flagship product or a commercial campaign.

After this final salutation, we all went our way, with a light heart and a heavy stomach.

This might become a new tradition in Osaka!...

# LVMH - Explore the LOEWE x My Neighbor Totoro collaboration

Inspired by Hayao Miyazaki’s film masterpiece My Neighbor Totoro , the latest capsule collection from Loewe celebrates the love of craft shared by the celebrated Spanish luxury house and Studio Ghibli.

The result, LOEWE x My Neighbor Totoro, transports the protagonists of the movie onto a range of clothing, leather bags and accessories. The collection celebrates the poetry and immediacy of these characters’ iconography – qualities have made My Neighbor Totoro a true cultural landmark.

Studio Ghibli was a natural choice for Loewe’s latest collaboration given their mutual love of artisanal techniques.

The characters and images in the film have become timeless icons marked by poetic animation, fantastical adventures, environmental message and magnificent soundtracks. For Loewe Creative Director Jonathan Anderson, My Neighbor Totoro is the ultimate in heartwarming entertainment. The designer finds the friendship of the young heroines with the king of the forest, the magical Totoro and his mischievous susuwatari dust bunnies who can’t be seen by adults especially touching.

Characters from the animated film come to life on leather accessories such as wallets and pouches, plus the iconic LOEWE Puzzle, Balloon and Hammock bags. Tote bags are embellished with a tapestry technique, drawing on meticulous craftsmanship to recreate the world of My Neighbor Totoro. Studio Ghibli’s original drawings are interpreted for this collaboration with Loewe as prints, leather marquetry and jacquard intarsia, giving the collection a timeless and mythic feel.

“The message is one of dreamy serenity and hands-on creativity – of being at one with nature and with one’s own inner child,” says Jonathan Anderson. “This is especially important right now and, I think, always will be,” adds the designer. The LOEWE x My Neighbor Totoro collection is available in a limited edition at Loewe points of sale worldwide, including Le Bon Marché in Paris.

# Madoka no Mori in Gōra, Hakone: a sustainable stay that awakens both the mind and the senses

Located conveniently close to Tokyo, Gora in Hakone is nestled within lush natural surroundings. Here, you’ll find a traditional Japanese inn advocating a new concept of "Green Luxury"—this is Madoka no Mori . This inn upholds a philosophy of harmony with nature and contribution to a sustainable future. A stay here promises a one-of-a-kind experience that stimulates intellectual curiosity and deeply soothes the body and mind.

The Spirit and Philosophy Behind Madoka no Mori

Since its opening in 2014, Madoka no Mori has prioritized building meaningful "connections" with its guests—a value reflected in its very name. Hospitality infused with a "round heart" (a play on the word “Madoka,” meaning round or harmonious) provides each visitor with a warm, attentive, and sincere experience.

Madoka no Mori is more than just a place to stay; it embodies a philosophy of connecting people with nature and the future—a place where new value is born.

Living in Harmony with Nature: The Origin

The inn’s deep commitment to the environment was catalyzed by a major natural disaster in 2019. As a result of this disaster, the historic Sounkaku , which had been in operation since 1925, was forced to close. However, this event became a turning point that deepened the recognition of nature’s power, blessings, and preciousness.

Since then, Madoka no Mori has pursued a vision of a sustainable inn that lives in gratitude and harmony with the natural world.

A Culinary Experience that Opens the Future: Innovative Hydrogen Cooking

The cuisine at Madoka no Mori combines environmental consciousness with supreme flavor through an innovative method— hydrogen cooking . At the in-house restaurant Kappo Mugen , this CO₂-free cooking technique enhances the natural umami of seasonal ingredients.

# Maison Duculty : a successful export story

Renowned for its outstanding charcuterie, Maison Duculty turned to the Business Support service of CCI France Japan to enter the Japanese market.

Charcutiers for several generations, Maison Duculty has been producing high quality charcuterie in the Lyon region for many years.

Having long held a personal interest in Japan, Gaëtan Duculty, Managing Director of the company, turned his attention to this market with the aim of sharing his products in Japan. Quickly faced with the difficulties of importing such products and it should be recalled that Japanese regulations are very strict when it comes to charcuterie he decided to call on the Business Support service of CCI France Japan to assist him in his efforts.

## A prospecting mission tailored to his sector

Thanks to his region’s Go Export program, he was able to quickly identify his needs. CCI France Japan then organized business meetings for him during the France Week event, which brings together French product exporters at the renowned Isetan department store in Tokyo.

“ CCI prepared eight highly qualified business meetings for me. This allowed me to very precisely identify the work that needed to be done in order to import my products. It was also an opportunity to establish contacts with importers, an essential gateway to selling my products in Japan ”, Gaëtan Duculty tells us.

Upon his return, he wasted no time and complied with the country’s requirements. He quickly implemented the expected standards along the production chain and prepared an application for approval.

Exports are still exclusive and limited to the hotel and restaurant sector, but Gaëtan Duculty hopes to soon be able to distribute his products to the Japanese general public. He was also present at the French Week organized at Isetan, where his charcuterie products enjoyed real success with Japanese consumers.

# Message from the President of the CCI France Japon

The CCI France Japan is deeply saddened by the news of the death, in tragic circumstances, of former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe.

Few Japanese leaders have meant as much to France as Shinzo Abe. The former Prime Minister saw the country as an anchor in Europe, but also as a bridge to Africa and a vital voice at the United Nations. He had a sincere familiarity with his French interlocutors, from all walks of life, which greatly benefited diplomatic, commercial and simply human exchanges between our two countries.

Fighting against the protectionist forces at work in his opposition and even in his own inner circle, Shinzo Abe used much of his political capital to impose the historic JEFTA (Japan-EU Free Trade Agreement) between his country and the European Union, which came into force in 2019, with French companies among the beneficiaries. "The signing of the economic partnership agreement has so far had a positive impact on France's foreign trade with Japan (significant increase in wine and dairy exports), even if its full implementation remains an issue (residual presence of non-tariff barriers). During the first ten months following its entry into force, French exports to Japan (+18%) outperformed European exports, which were almost stable (6%). Trade has increased in both directions and the effects of the agreement are perceived positively on the Japanese side," notes the Senate in an April 2021 report.

As an enthusiastic supporter of the triennial TICAD conference, which brings together Japan and dozens of African countries, he understood the decisive role of France on this continent.

Wishing to raise Japan's role at the UN by obtaining a seat as a permanent member of its Security Council, Shinzo Abe had found support in France. He also recognized in France, the only European power with a large military presence in the Indo-Pacific, an important partner in maintaining security in "his" region of the world.

# Message from the President of the CCI France Japon

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/message-from-the-president-of-the-cci-france-japon.html
The sheer number of times that Shinzo Abe visited France attests to the importance that he attached to that country. "It had been seven years since a Japanese head of government had visited France. Seven years ago, his name was already Shinzo Abe," said François Hollande when he received him in Paris in 2014, referring to his first stint as prime minister in 2007. Until 2019, Shinzo Abe visited Paris at least once a year to meet his French counterpart.

But it was on the economic and cultural level that the relationship was richest. Shinzo Abe saw France, the world's leading tourist destination, as a "gateway" that would place his country at the top of the list of "destinations". Thus, he had initiated, and richly endowed, a year of Japanese cultural events in France in 2018, under the title "Japonismes". Other popular world events are also taking place, in France and Japan consecutively: the Rugby World Cup, in Japan in 2019 and then in France in 2023; the Olympic and Paralympic Games in Japan in 2021, then in France in 2024.

This was the meaning of the renewal in 2013 of the "exceptional partnership" between France and Japan, a document that frames and encourages Franco-Japanese relations and whose three axes are, in order: economy, security, culture. Its "roadmap" is due to be renewed in 2023.

In Japan, his voluntarist policy known as "Abenomics" revived economic activity and benefited the member companies of the CCI France Japon.

In the hope of the future fruits of this work, we send our most sincere condolences, in these tragic circumstances, to the family and friends of Shinzo Abe.

Jérôme Chouchan, president of the CCI France Japon

# Montblanc: the centenary of the Meisterstück collection

Montblanc’s iconic Meisterstück celebrates its 100th anniversary this year.

Richemont Japan K.K. This year, Montblanc celebrates the centenary of the Meisterstück, a veritable jewel in the culture of writing.

The origins of Montblanc

Contrary to what the Montblanc brand name might suggest, the company was founded in Germany at the beginning of the 20th century.

Three friends from Hamburg (Alfred Nehemias, August Eberstein and Claus Voss) met regularly to exchange ideas. It was during these discussions that they came up with the idea of creating a pen with its own ink reservoir .

The first “fountain pen” model was born after three years of intense research, with the launch of the “Rouge et Noir” collection, echoing the game of roulette. The project was a rapid success, leading the three friends to register their own trademark: the Montblanc brand was born.

The name Montblanc was chosen because the brand would be, in the words of its creators, “the pinnacle of writing instruments.” The visual identity and logo reinforce this ambition, with a white six-pointed star referring to the six glaciers of the mountain range.

Morphée+ , founded on May 3, 2018 in Dijon, develops and markets the electromagnetic device of the same name: a real-time monitoring and fall detection system that enhances the safety and well-being of residents in nursing homes (EHPAD – Residential Care Facilities for Dependent Elderly People) as well as patients living at home.

# Itinéraires singuliers – Cyril Coppini: From a Passion for Kanji to the Stage of the Olympia, 25 Years of Performance and Translation in Japan

Cyril Coppini could have become a Japanese language teacher in France. Instead, the life of the southern French native took an unexpected turn when he discovered rakugo, the traditional Japanese storytelling art that originated during the Edo period, in which a lone performer kneels on a cushion to tell humorous or dramatic stories.

Today, as a renowned manga translator, including the famous Detective Conan, and the only French rakugo performer based in Japan, he embodies a unique cultural bridge between France and Japan.

“Whatever choices we make, we will always face obstacles. So we might as well devote our energy to what truly matters to us.”

Falling in Love with the Japanese Language

Cyril Coppini discovered Japanese as a teenager, almost by chance, after choosing it as an elective subject at school. From his very first lesson, he was captivated by the beauty and complexity of Japanese writing.

Soon afterwards, he visited Japan for the first time through a school exchange program. There, he experienced firsthand the gap between the Japanese taught in classrooms and the language spoken in everyday life, while discovering the country's remarkable cultural and linguistic richness.

He went on to pursue advanced studies in Japanese before returning to live in Japan. Despite his strong academic background, he came to realize that true language mastery is acquired above all through daily life and direct interaction with local people.

Rakugo: From Osaka to the Olympia

Cyril Coppini first discovered rakugo on television. In 2009, he began studying the art in Osaka while continuing his professional career. Two years later, he gave his first public performance. As he did not follow the traditional apprenticeship required of professional Japanese rakugo storytellers, he describes himself as a "rakugo performer" rather than a master, a position that gives him greater creative freedom when introducing the art abroad.

# Itinéraires singuliers – Cyril Coppini: From a Passion for Kanji to the Stage of the Olympia, 25 Years of Performance and Translation in Japan

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/n.html
His work as a translator, where rendering Japanese humour and wordplay presents constant challenges, has led him to reject literal translation in favour of thoughtful cultural adaptation. This experience has also enabled him to tailor his performances to audiences in multiple languages.

From 2016 onwards, he began adapting and translating his stories for non-Japanese-speaking audiences. Their enthusiastic reception demonstrated that rakugo's distinctive humour and storytelling tradition can resonate with audiences around the world.

He notably delivered a memorable performance at the Olympia in Paris, a venue comparable in prestige to Japan's National Theatre stages. In 2025, he also performed at the France Pavilion during Expo 2025 Osaka, bringing his stories to life before a predominantly Japanese audience.

25 Years in Japan and Looking Ahead

After more than 25 years in Japan, Cyril Coppini has witnessed the country's gradual internationalisation. Today, he also performs in English to meet the growing interest of international audiences eager to discover rakugo. His ambition is to keep the art alive beyond its traditional settings, which can sometimes feel inaccessible to younger generations, notably by developing masterclasses.

For Cyril Coppini, the most important thing is to pursue what one truly loves while accepting that the journey will inevitably be filled with challenges. In his view, the pursuit of absolute stability is an illusion. After all, the stories of mistakes and failures often become the funniest ones to tell, provided that we continue moving forward with our goals firmly in sight.

He concludes:

“Deep down, nobody really knows what stability is. That's precisely why it's better to follow the path that genuinely draws you. That doesn't mean wandering aimlessly for years, though. It's important to have a clear direction, a core conviction that guides your decisions.”

# Nailmatic : a young, innovative cosmetics company 100% made in France

Company overview

Nailmatic is a young, innovative cosmetics company 100% made in France, founded in Paris in November 2012. This Paris based company quickly stood out from its competitors thanks to the unprecedented creation of a vending machine used to sell its nail polishes. But that is not all. Beyond this original distribution concept, the company also offers ethical and eco responsible products.

Shortly after the launch of its first vending machine at the Citadium Paris store in 2012, Nailmatic ’s “color vending machine” began to find its place in major Parisian department stores such as Printemps Haussmann, BHV Le Marais, and Galeries Lafayette. In 2014, Nailmatic was awarded by the Paris Dauphine Commercial Innovation Observatory, receiving the prize for best customer strategy. That same year, the company decided to launch a new product range specifically designed for children, featuring responsible and bio sourced formulas.

What about Japan?

“We began to take an interest in exporting in 2015. As Japan is the reference country when it comes to vending machines, exporting our products there seemed like an obvious choice,” explains Stéphane Philip, Export Manager at Nailmatic .

Aware of the complexity of the Japanese market, Nailmatic turned directly to CCI France Japan in its search for a new partner to distribute its women’s product range in Japan. Following its request, CCI France Japan proposed an individual mission in February 2016, which led to several meetings with three different prospects, including National Vending Co LTD. Since that initial meeting, Nailmatic has built strong ties and maintained a solid relationship of trust with this partner, notably through multiple meetings in France and in Japan. “We would not have been able to build these relationships so easily without the help of our on site translator and interpreter,” Stéphane Philip emphasizes.

# Nearly 40% of payments in Japan are now cashless

Cashless payments have increased by 3 percentage points compared to 2022.

Cashless payment methods (credit cards, transport cards, QR codes, debit cards) are on the rise in Japan.

According to a survey published on March 29 by the Japan Credit Association, cashless payment methods increased year-on-year, involving payments of 126,000 billion yen (around 771 billion euros).

These payment methods were popularized during the Covid pandemic . Today, they are up 12 percentage points in 2019 (28.8% of transactions).

The acceleration of cashless payments is a matter of public policy in Japan, with a stated government target of 40% of total transactions by 2025 .

There are many challenges to the adoption of cashless payments . The use of digital payment methods frees up labor in a country where it is in short supply.

The evolution of payment infrastructures has also helped to popularize this practice: a large number of payment methods can now be managed by a single machine, as can the choice of payment methods in stores.

However, the increase in cashless payment methods also means an increase in fraud, which will amount to 54 billion yen (nearly 330 million euros) in 2023 alone.

Japan still lags behind its neighbors : 80% of payments are cashless in China and 90% in Korea. In the United States and the United Kingdom, the figure is also over 50%.

# “OECD Education2030 Project Infinity": international collaboration for tomorrow's schools

​​​​​​​Après le succès du “Tohoku Appeal Event” en 2024, c’est au tour de la “OECD Education2030 Project Infinity” !

After the success of the “Tohoku Appeal Event” in 2024, it's the turn of the “OECD Education2030 Project Infinity”!

Following the earthquake on March 11, 2011, in Japan and the ensuing nuclear accident, Fukushima University, the Japanese Ministry of Education, Science and Technology and the OECD decided to create the “Tohoku School” , days dedicated to sharing and bringing students together.

Above all, these events enabled children who had lived through the disaster to make new friends, to rebuild the school as a place to live, to rediscover the essential values of life, and to build a new world based on the use of renewable energies.

The project culminated in an event in August 2014 - the Tohoku Appeal Event in Paris - which took place on the Champs de Mars in Paris. Students from all over the world mobilized for the occasion. The event was introduced by a speech from the city of Paris,the Japanese Ambassador to France as well as representatives from the OECD. The days were punctuated by animations, dances, cultural events (Tachibana)...

10 years on, the OECD has decided to carry out a new project for education: “OECD Education2030 Project Infinity.” The project was led by students from Japan and Canada. Its aim is to enable students from different countries to create collaborative products, which could help improve well-being at school and within communities.

The project currently involves 112 schools in 24 countries, with 30 Japanese schools taking part . A Summit for the project will be held this December at the OECD offices , to present the products created in collaboration and discuss future education with actors from around the world, based on the real experiences of students and teachers through “Project Infinity.”

Founded in 1979 , ONIS is a company specializing in the design and manufacture of equipment dedicated to industrial piping operations. For more than forty years , the company has been developing solutions that enable fast , safe , and repeatable interventions, carried out by a single operator and requiring no tools. With over 12,000 devices deployed worldwide , ONIS has built a strong reputation for reliability, supported by an international network of engineers committed to continuously improving the safety, performance, and profitability of industrial assets.

The company’s flagship product, the Quick Action Line Blind (QLB), is designed to replace spectacle blinds and figure-eight blinds. The QLB ensures absolute isolation between upstream and downstream, without the use of bolts or nuts. It therefore guarantees optimal sealing while significantly reducing downtime during line blinding operations.

Designed for critical applications, ONIS solutions primarily serve the oil and gas sector , including refineries, compression units, and pipeline management systems. They are capable of operating under extreme conditions , ranging from –120°C to 650°C and up to 420 bar (6,000 PSI).

# Over 3 million tourists visited Japan in March, an all-time record

This is the highest number achieved for a single month, surpassing the 2,991,100 visitors in July 2019.

According to a survey conducted by the National Tourism Organization, the number of Japanese tourists was 3.08 million in March , the highest number ever recorded for a single month, surpassing the 2,991,100 visitors who visited Japan in July 2019.

Tourists from South Korea were the most numerous, followed by visitors from Taiwan, China and the USA.

“Of the 23 countries and regions surveyed, 17 recorded a record number of visitors in March. We are closely monitoring the number of tourists from China, which remains at around 70% of its pre-pandemic level,” said the Japan National Tourism Organization.

The cherry blossom season and the depreciation of the yen are said to have been the main reasons for the increase in tourists.

In addition, tourist spending per traveler is around 209,000 yen, more than 60,000 yen higher than the same period in 2019. The Japan Tourism Agency attributes these figures to the impact of the weak yen, as well as to an increase in the number of days spent in Japan.

# Panel Discussion about Diversity and Inclusion in Japanese companies, from the point of view of 3 Women leaders in the Air Transport industry

On December 5th 2023, a significant event gathering 3 women leaders in the aerospace industry!

Panel Discussion about Diversity and Inclusion in Japanese companies, from the point of view of 3 Women leaders in the Air Transport industry.

"We had never considered that French women faced challenges in reaching managerial positions similar to those in Japan. We thought we were the only ones dealing with such issues."

On December 5th, 2023, a significant event unfolded at the Nagoya Innovators' Garage , located in Nadya Park. The gathering, which brought together professionals and individuals, focused on empowering women and promoting leadership roles. The event featured 3 prestigious speakers: Ms Béatrice Delpuech , Director Japan/Korea for Air France Cargo , Ms. Mayumi Ejima , General Manager of ANA ’s Nagoya Branch, and Ms. Junko Sakihara , General Manager of JAL ’s Chubu Branch Office.

The event kicked off with Béatrice Delpuech’s speech. She outlined her background with insights into her remarkable achievements with Sodexi , Air France and Air France Cargo .

She went on sharing her views on maintaining a work-life balance, addressing the differences between the working environments for women in France, Amsterdam ( KLM ), and Japan, and exposing AF methods to increase the representation of women in male-dominated sectors, such as logistics.

A talk session between the three guest speakers followed the seminar.

# Panel Discussion about Diversity and Inclusion in Japanese companies, from the point of view of 3 Women leaders in the Air Transport industry

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/panel-discussion-about-diversity-and-inclusion-in-japanese-companies-from-the-point-of-view-of-3-women-leaders-in-the-air-transport-industry.html
A talk session between the three guest speakers followed the seminar.

After being invited to reflect on the impactful points of Béatrice's presentation, the other two speakers Junko Sakihara and Mayumi Ejima shared their own thoughts on the question, offering understanding into the promotion of female leadership at JAL and ANA, respectively. The talk session took an unexpected turn as the speakers shared their surprise at the revelation that France, perceived by many as progressive, is still grappling with issues of gender inclusivity. The realization sparked a dynamic conversation, and shed light on the need for continuous efforts to address gender disparities in various professional spheres, even in seemingly advanced societies. The event ended with a networking session, where everyone could share their thoughts with the speakers.

If we could pinpoint one key moment, it would undoubtedly be when Béatrice Delpuech made an observation regarding the self-imposed barriers that women often place on their professional aspirations. She noted that, due to fear and a lack of self-confidence, many women hesitate to accept well-deserved positions, driven by the enduring belief that aspects like marriage or pregnancy might hinder their professional success.

In conclusion, our heartfelt gratitude extends to the Central Japan Economic Federation for their steadfast support. A special appreciation is due as well to Haruka Mizuta from IBA for her live translation, and finally we also thank sincerely the MOF (Meilleur Ouvriers de France) organization for their sponsorship, allowing participants to enjoy Nespresso coffee during the event. Each of them was also able to take home a delightful treat—a bag of bread from Gifu's delectable bakery, ' Guruman Vital '.

# PARSYS : Telemedecal solution

In 2023, as part of a collective mission organized by CCI France Japon and Business France, in partnership with the Ile de France Region, the telemedicine company Parsys, along with other companies from the Île-de-France region, benefited from a prospecting mission in Japan.

This was the second mission for Parsys, the first having taken place in 2021. This mission provided an opportunity for Parsys to meet new prospects and establish new partnerships. Following this mission, and after several years of operation, Parsys finally concluded a partnership with Sharemedical, a Japanese company in the telehealth and medical devices sector.

"Penetrating the Japanese market proves challenging for French companies due to significant barriers such as language and cultural differences. Faced with these challenges, many hesitate to engage in it. Moreover, to succeed in this market, it is crucial to offer an innovative solution. If a similar solution already exists, Japanese companies generally prefer a local option due to ease of communication, local support, and absence of time zone differences. My personal experience perfectly illustrates these obstacles.

Upon my arrival in Japan, I attempted to contact Japanese prospects without success. I then sought assistance from CCIFJ for an initial prospecting mission, which allowed me to secure several meetings, including one with a company to which I had previously sent multiple unanswered messages. It was during this meeting that I made my first contact with Sharemedical. Subsequently, we remained in contact with Sharemedical's president, but without finalizing a collaboration project. Last November's mission was decisive. Thanks to the work and support of my project leader, Ms. Takahara, and my translator, Ms. Miki, we were able to overcome the final obstacles and finalize a partnership agreement between our two companies."

# People Analytics: Big Data is HR’s next frontier

The second HR Committee of 2019 on 18th July dealt with the subject of big data and its applications in human resources. 30 participants from a wide range of companies listened as Peter Romero, People Analytics Lead at the Cambridge Psychometrics Centre of the University of Cambridge, UK, talked them through why and how HR needed to become “quantitative”. By using numerous examples and documented thought-provoking figures (e.g. 82% of managers are misplaced, 13% of employees are engaged), Peter explained in particular how People Analytics can help organizations make better leader selections and raise any alarm bells early on as to which profiles might be unfit for the role. Peter also gave tips as to how even smaller companies can kick-start People Analytics using off-the-shelf tools.

Adding to the many applications of People Analytics, Fabien Roudier, Senior Manager at Institution for a Global Society Corporation (IGS), explained how its application GROW360 uses data analysis and machine learning in optimizing recruitment processes. Again, using the example of a large Japanese corporation, Fabien showed how to remove selection bias and make sure the best candidates are selected based on their soft skills assessment and on continuously improving predictive models of who will be a top-performer.

The CCI France Japon wishes to thank the speakers, participants and president of the HR Committee, Grégory Dancs, for a successful and very informative session.

# Podcast Itinéraires Singuliers – From Strasbourg to Tokyo: The Journey of Jérôme Guth, Head Coach of Japan's Olympic Sabre Fencing Teams

A French fencing enthusiast falls in love with Japan and leads the national team to a historic Olympic medal in Paris. The podcast Itinéraires Singuliers opens its first episode with the story of Jérôme Guth – Head Coach of Japan's Men's and Women's Olympic Sabre Fencing Teams – and what it reveals about the business of sport in Japan.

Born in Strasbourg, he discovered fencing at the age of six and met a fencing master who would mark his entire life. This charismatic, demanding, and caring mentor passed on his love for the sabre – a passion that would stay with Jérôme forever. After serious studies and an early career as a high-level referee, Jérôme moved to the United States at 25, first to complete his studies, then to open his own club. America taught him entrepreneurship, freedom, and the power of believing in his dreams – even if the “all-business” logic eventually made him crave something else.

It was then that Japan entered his story. After several brief but deeply impactful trips, he accepted the role of head coach for the Japanese national sabre team. Arriving during the Covid period, he had to wait before settling in, but once there, he transformed the team’s dynamic. With caring management, Olympic-level rigor, and profound respect for local culture, he restored confidence in his athletes and achieved historic results.

The pinnacle: the 2024 Paris Olympic Games. In a packed Grand Palais, his fencers accomplished the extraordinary by winning a bronze medal against France, the world number one team. Immense joy, shared without restraint, became a turning point for Japanese sabre.

But Jérôme didn’t stop there. With the medal in hand, he was already looking ahead to Los Angeles 2028. His mission: continue growing the team, develop young talent through the Elite Academy, and firmly establish Japan among the world’s leading fencing nations.

## — Hike through the primitive forests of Yanbaru

Yanbaru is northern Okinawa’s mountainous region of primeval forests and rare endemic wildlife. Among its native subtropical flora are epiphytic ferns and orchids, living fossil cycads, giant banyans, evergreen Itajii, and the famous towering Okinawa Urajirogashi tree on Mt. Ibudake. Endemic species of fauna include the iconic Yanbaru kuina (Okinawa Rail), Noguchi gera (Okinawa Woodpecker), Ryukyu yamagame (Ryukyu Black Breasted Leaf Turtle). Hike up to cloud forests on Mt. Yonahadake, admire spectacular views from limestone cliffs overlooking Shioya Bay, or follow a scenic trail leading to the 26-meter drop of Hiji Otaki Falls.

## — Discover the Romance of Kouri Island

If limiting interaction with others while slow traveling remains a concern, consider renting a bicycle in Nago and going for a refreshing ride along Kouri Island - it’s a highly charismatic destination for lovers, featuring the timeless attraction of a coralline rock formation in the shape of a heart, which is also the setting of Okinawa’s own Adam and Eve legend. From Nago, turn off Route 58 onto Yagaji Island, then continue across to Kouri Bridge, savoring each scenic minute of its 1,960-meter span over clear turquoise water. On the other side, enjoy touring the coastline with more luscious sea views around Kouri Island’s 8-kilometer circumference.

Wherever and however you choose to travel through the islands, keep in mind that the less populated, more wild region of northern Okinawa offers a variety of secluded retreats and safe activities for both a socially distanced workspace and a splendid vacation.

An Employment Adjustment Subsidy ("Koyouchousei-jyoseikin") is provided for an employer, who has been forced to reduce business activities due to the effects of Covid-19 and temporarily suspended work, or who has trained or dispatched employees in order to maintain their employment, for some of the leave allowance paid to employees.

# Real wages fall for 23rd consecutive month in Japan

Wage increases have failed to keep pace with inflation: this is the longest decline on record.

According to government data released on Monday, real wages in Japan fell for the 23rd consecutive month .

With Prime Minister Fumio Kishida calling on business leaders to raise wages at a rate below inflation, the country equaled its longest period of real wage decline since 1991, with a 1.3% drop in February.

The last such decline occurred between 2007 and 2009 , during the global financial crisis.

However, real wages have lagged behind price rises, essential to overcoming the deflationary stagnation that has prevailed since the 90s. Households’ purchasing power is declining, while the price of everyday consumer goods continues to rise due to rising raw material costs and the weak yen.

The impact of higher starting salaries at major Japanese companies will be reflected in the future.

Tax-free sales in supermarkets were 2.4 times higher than in the same month last year.

Sales of tax-free products in supermarkets increased by a factor of 2.4 in March 2024 compared with the same period last year . This record figure is attributable to the weakening yen and the upturn in tourism,

According to a report published by the Japan Superstore Association, sales amounted to 510.9 billion yen last month, an increase of around 1% on the same month of the previous year. This was the 25th consecutive month of growth.

Among the sales of large stores, tax-free sales amounted to 49.5 billion yen, 2.4 times higher than in the same month last year. This is the highest record since 2014, when the surveys began.

“The weak yen is very beneficial for foreign customers,” said Japan Superstore Association CEO Yoko Yasuda . However, she remains cautious: “if the yen weakens further, Japanese customers could enter a phase where it [will be] difficult to buy.”

# Remote work on the decline in Japan

The results of a survey conducted by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism were published on March 31.

Remote work practices, made widespread by the Covid-19 pandemic, are on the decline in Japan . These are the findings of an online survey conducted by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism between November and December 2023 on a sample of 40,000 people.

In the course of 2023, 26.1% of respondents indicated that they teleworked, a decrease of 0.9 percentage points compared to 2022. This proportion varies by region. For example, almost 40% of respondents working in Tokyo telework, compared with 17.5% in the regions.

However, it seems that work patterns combining telecommuting and presence in the workplace are on the increase .

The frequency of employed teleworkers intending to continue working is high. The main reasons are “efficient use of time” (around 40% of respondents) and “reduced commuting time” (around 33% of respondents).

# Results Survey on the “Reaction Of The European Business Community In Japan To COVID-19 Crisis And Impact On Its Operations”

This survey has been designed by the European Business Council in Japan and sent to the 18 European National Chambers of Commerce in Japan, who kindly circulated it among their Members. Industry was given between February 26th to March 10th, 2020 to answer the questionnaire. The data was collected anonymously.

In February 2020, the European Union and Japan celebrated the first anniversary of the entry into force of the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA). According to a European Commission Press Release, “in the first ten months following the implementation of the agreement, EU exports to Japan went up by 6.6% compared to the same period the year before.”

In this context of increased exchanges between the EU and Japan, the objective of this survey is to better understand the current situation at European companies operating in Japan confronted to the COVID-19 crisis and to highlight its direct impact on their economic activity.

SUMMARY

260 companies from 16 EU countries answered the survey. 82% of them introduced changes to their working style to protect their employees by implementing specific measures such as restrictions on business trips (76%) and public events (55%). Telework is an interesting option for most of them (70%).

The impact on turnover for the first semester 2020 is generally revised downwards: 35% of the respondents expect a 20% decline, but 38% stress their lack of visibility.

# A look back at our Dinner Seminar at the Morikawa Salon:

This Thursday, July 16, we held an event that has been organized in years past with the Morikawa Clinic: a dinner seminar, this year themed around “The Art de Vivre.”

Participants gathered for a convivial evening at the Morikawa Lounge in Amagasaki, whose decor is inspired by the French elegance of the Marie Antoinette era . The event began with a presentation on the Art de Vivre, exploring various themes that highlighted the connections and influences between French and Japanese cultures.

During this presentation, the benefits of roses were highlighted: by using all of our senses, we can enjoy their many virtues, such as relaxation, improved circulation, and stress relief, among others. We can experience these blessings through a wide variety of products : beverages, jams, oils, and other rose-based preparations. Guests also had the opportunity to try several of these products during dinner.

The seminar then continued with a focus on the health benefits of tea . Ms. Morikawa shared her expertise as a Kampō Tea Master (herbal teas derived from traditional Chinese medicine). She highlighted the properties of various plants and how they can be used to promote everyday well-being.

In the spirit of this philosophy, Salon Morikawa will soon open its doors as a tea lounge . It will feature a space dedicated to exploring tea and rose-based products, in keeping with the "art de vivre" philosophy presented during the seminar.

Following this enriching presentation, a French buffet was served to the participants , who enjoyed refined cuisine while continuing their discussions. Conversations quickly became lively, fostering wonderful connections and a warm atmosphere that made this reception a particularly enjoyable occasion for exchange.

A big thank you to all our participants for their attendance and enthusiasm, we also warmly thank the Morikawa Clinic for its invaluable support and commitment to working alongside us in organizing this dinner seminar.

# A look back at our seminar Craftsmanship: Cross Perspectives France × Japan :

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/retour-sur-le-seminaire-metiers-dart-expertises-croisees-france-japon.html
Kansai Event report

# A look back at our seminar Craftsmanship: Cross Perspectives France × Japan :

Three panel discussions , each exploring one of the major issues ; seven inspiring and inspired speakers ; a lively networking buffet ; and nearly 100 delighted participants who traveled specifically from Tokyo, Ishikawa, and Fukuoka: here is a glimpse into the success of this first collaboration in Kyoto between the Institut Français du Kansai and the Kansai Office of the CCI France Japon, focusing on the important topic of traditional crafts and their future in the current socio-economic context .

On June 18, 2026, the Institut Français du Kansai hosted the first event dedicated to the evolution of craftsmanship practices between France and Japan . The first session focused on the numerous opportunities for modernization offered by the digital transformation of businesses . We explored two key areas in particular: internal management systems , on the one hand, and methods for distributing craft products —particularly logistics—on the other.

We were able to learn from the systems introduced and implemented by Pierre Vauvy to rationalize the internal operations of the family-owned business , Okayama Kōgei , particularly in order management (more than 500 fabrics tracked in real time), the indexing of design patterns (more than 20,000 references), and customer relations (real-time color-matching tests for patterns via video conferencing).

Meanwhile, Thomas Bertrand has worked with Ship&Co over the past two decades to develop highly effective logistics solutions for large-scale international shipping . He has also shared his insights with us regarding online visibility and the importance of a combined physical presence. The time savings generated by these solutions allow artisans to spend more time focusing on the creative process .

# A look back at our seminar Craftsmanship: Cross Perspectives France × Japan :

url: https://www.ccifj.or.jp/en/publications/news/news-detail/news/retour-sur-le-seminaire-metiers-dart-expertises-croisees-france-japon.html
International outreach was also at the heart of the discussion between Kōtarō Nishibori and Ema Okamoto during the second roundtable, which focused on opening up artisanal excellence to the international market . In addition to efforts to introduce foreign customers to traditional Japanese craftsmanship,this process of renewal first began within Japan through interactions with other creative fields. The curiosity of both speakers led them to rethink Japanese design and cultural norms , paving the way for new collaborations with foreign artists and breaking into new markets that were previously considered saturated.

Finally, the seminar ended with a remarkable presentation by Toma Yamazoe , Mayuko Sano , and Emina Morioka on the process of transcreation of cultural resources: the challenge of transforming heritage into new value . Drawing on their respective roles in the political, academic, and private sectors, these three speakers demonstrated how the implementation of innovations and initiatives on a global scale is driven by the commitment and engagement of both private and government stakeholders.

Following the final panel discussion, Ms. Sandrine Mouchet , Consul General of France in Kyoto and Director of the Institut Français du Kansai, concluded the seminar by highlighting the essential role of traditional crafts in strengthening the ties between France and Japan.

Each of these actors plays a significant role in fostering trends that are well suited to the economic landscape, with the key players being the local residents and artisans , without whom a healthy ecosystem that benefits everyone cannot exist.

Following these roundtable discussions, the French and Japanese participants continued their discussions throughout the evening, with the generous support of our sponsors Mouton Cadet and Veuve Clicquot , over an exceptional French buffet showcasing the tastes of France.

Thank you all for your enthusiastic participation in this seminar , which proves that the far too often neglected topic of traditional craftsmanship deserves renewed attention. We look forward to your continued involvement, ideas, and future efforts to help develop it further!

# Looking Back at The French Brand Design Seminar, Fukui Desk

On June 16, the CCIFJ Fukui Desk organized a seminar dedicated to brand concept creation.

After a brief presentation of the Chamber’s activities by our Regional Offices Director, we had the honor of welcoming Ms. Virginie Lefevre, CCIFJ Ambassador in Fukui, who shared her vision of how a brand can stand out through its craftsmanship and know-how.

Designer and entrepreneur, Ms. Lefevre is the founder of the brand Viruxiny. She began her career as a designer for major international fashion houses in Paris, London, Canada, and the United States. Twenty-five years ago, she moved to Japan to teach fashion at ESMOD Tokyo, before eventually settling there permanently.

Based in Fukui for the past 19 years, she founded her own company and has developed a brand that is entirely locally produced. Her creations are now distributed in major department stores such as Isetan, Hankyu, and Mitsukoshi through pop-up sales across Japan. She also works as a freelancer with several local companies and is actively involved in the region’s cultural and media scene, including campaigns such as the Pink Ribbon initiative on Fukui TV, interviews with NHK, and various local publications.

Fukui is a particularly attractive region where traditional craftsmanship coexists with innovative companies that are oriented toward international markets.

The conference was followed by a Q&A session, allowing participants to further explore the topics discussed and ask questions to the speakers.

These exchanges were greatly appreciated and continued in a friendly atmosphere during the networking session that concluded the event.

We would like to take this opportunity to express our sincere thanks to Fukui Prefecture for its support in organizing this event.

# Highlights from our tasting evening featuring rums from France’s overseas territories.

Organized in collaboration with J'imagine Japan, the event featured students from Martinique, Réunion and other regions currently undertaking internships in Japan through the organization's program.

Through their presentations, these young talents offered participants an immersion into the world of sugar cane, from the origins of rum in France’s overseas territories to the diversity of French rum traditions. Guiding guests through a tasting of 12 rums from Martinique and Réunion, the students explained the distinctive characteristics of each spirit, from terroirs and production methods to tasting notes and serving recommendations. The experience was complemented by a selection of specialties from the French overseas territories, including fresh tropical fruits and accras, offering participants a true culinary journey.

# Seminar Recap: Exporting Wagashi to France

Artisan perspectives, market insights, regulatory challenges, innovation in the use of kanten, and support for companies expanding internationally.

We were pleased to welcome nearly 60 participants , including around 15 who joined online . Among them were professionals connecting from Tokyo, as well as students from the French National Institute for Oriental Languages and Civilizations ( Inalco ) , who were able to follow the seminar via a live stream with automatically generated subtitles.

The seminar opened with a presentation on the growing interest in Japanese culture among French audiences. Highlighting nearly 170 years of diplomatic relations between France and Japan, our master of ceremonies, Ms. MIZUTA Haruka , reflected on several milestones that have strengthened ties between the two countries, including Japonismes 2018 , French President Macron's visit to Japan last April, and the recent sumo tournament held in Paris .

Ms. MIZUTA also noted the steady increase in the number of French visitors traveling to Japan each year, as well as the growing presence of Japanese grocery stores and specialty wagashi shops across France. She then introduced the seminar's speakers, who shared their expertise and experiences with the audience.

## Two wagashi artisans share their experience

We were honored to welcome Mr. OKAMOTO Nobuharu , owner of the Kotoyo wagashi shop in Yokkaichi. We were also delighted to welcome Mr. MURATA Takanori , a Nagoya-born wagashi artisan now based in Paris, who joined the seminar online.

Drawing on their respective experiences, both speakers shared valuable insights into their craftsmanship and the challenges and opportunities of expanding their businesses internationally. Their firsthand perspectives provided participants with practical advice and inspiration for bringing traditional Japanese confectionery to overseas markets.

## Kanten: A promising ingredient for the European market

Expanding into international markets presents both opportunities and challenges. With this in mind, we were honored to welcome Ina Food Industry Co., Ltd. , a leading manufacturer of plant-based gelling agents derived from seaweed, better known as kanten .

# A look back at our guided tour, exploring Hakata-ori and the landscapes of Itoshima

On Friday, July 3, the CCIFJ Kyushu Office was pleased to organize a day dedicated to exploring the artisanal heritage and iconic landscapes of Fukuoka Prefecture. The six participants had the privilege of enjoying a beautiful sunny day, which provided ideal conditions for this cultural immersion in the heart of Itoshima.

We were delighted to welcome the participants alongside Mr. Kuroki at Kuroki Orimono , where they began the day with a presentation on this family-run business and its craftsmanship, passed down through several generations. They learned about the history of Hakata-ori, its weaving techniques, and the symbolism behind its traditional patterns.

During the workshop tour, participants were able to explore the entire obi-making process, from the creation of the weaving yarn to the final product. This behind-the-scenes look at the workshop highlighted the precision, technical skill, and passion that drive the artisans at Kuroki Orimono. Participants then took part in a weaving workshop, creating a sample obi that they were able to keep as a memento of the experience an activity that generated great enthusiasm. The visit concluded with a friendly get-together, followed by a tour of the workshop’s boutique, offering the opportunity to discover and purchase original Hakata-ori creations.

The group then gathered for a convivial lunch overlooking the magnificent Itoshima Bay, where they enjoyed a generous buffet featuring seafood specialties, sashimi, and tempura, all while taking in the stunning scenery. The afternoon continued in the heart of Itoshima with a tour of several local artisan shops offering souvenirs, clothing, and regional products, before wrapping up with a break at a local café featuring traditional Japanese architecture.

From learning about ancestral craftsmanship to meeting artisans, sampling local cuisine, and exploring Itoshima’s heritage, the day offered participants a rich and enjoyable cultural experience that was greatly appreciated by the entire group.

# Return on Event : Presentation J'imagine Japan

On December 10 , the Chūbu Office of the CCIFJ had the pleasure to organize in collaboration with the association J’imagine Japan , a seminar held at Nagoya University of Foreign Studies . The event brought together around twenty students and faculty members , with the aim of raising awareness among students about international mobility and its key challenges.

Until now, J’imagine Japan had focused primarily on promoting mobility opportunities for French-speaking students in Japan. During this seminar, the association presented and promoted its new program, which takes the opposite approach by offering internship opportunities in France to Japanese students .

Well established in the Kansai region, J’imagine Japan has for many years been actively strengthening ties between France and Japan in various ways. In particular, the association has provided French students with internship opportunities within Japanese companies, as well as immersive internships centered on Japanese culture, including courses at Japanese language schools .

The French model of long-term internships (lasting several months) remains largely unfamiliar in Japan, which explains why corporate internship opportunities for foreign students are relatively rare. This issue had already been addressed last year during a dedicated seminar . In addition to supporting French students, J’imagine Japan is now tackling the issue from the other direction by raising awareness among Japanese students , starting at the university level, of the benefits of the French internship model and by offering them the opportunity to experience it firsthand. We hope that this long-term effort to promote immersive, extended internships will ultimately help bring about a shift in mindset on this issue within Japanese society.

The students showed strong interest in the internship opportunities , which would allow them to stand out in their academic paths, even though such experiences remain uncommon in Japan.

This unique opportunity to gain international professional experience was met with great curiosity from the students, who asked numerous questions not only about the internships themselves, but also about Martinique , the home island of François Régina, a representative of J’imagine Japan, which remains largely unfamiliar to them.

# Robert Walters - Hybrid work: What is the ideal number of days to work in the office?

Over 4,800 professionals globally share their work style preferences

## Ideal number of days to work in the office: twice per week

Specialist recruitment consultancy Robert Walters surveyed more than 4,800 professionals globally, including 334 in Japan, to understanding their work style preferences and career plans for 2021. Among professionals in Japan, twice per week is the most ideal number of days to work in the office, followed by three days per week. Globally, twice a week was also the most popular response (30%).

19% of respondents in Japan said they prefer to continue working fully remote, slightly higher than the global average of 13%. Among Japanese professionals, 37% said they would reject a job offer if they had to work nearly 100% of the week in person at the office. Commuting (84%), flexible hours (60%), and flexibility on where to live (52%) are the main reasons why professionals are willing to give up the office day-to-day.

## Popularity of remote work: only 5% willing to go back to going to the office every day

Only 5% of Japanese professionals affirm that they would like to go back to the old normal of going to the office five times a week. Remote work has been positively accepted, with only 3% saying that they would refuse a job offer that was 100% remote. The top three reasons preventing them from accepting a fully remote role include: having the option to come to the office when you feel like it (54%), feeling more productive in the office (36%), and face-to-face meetings and social interaction with colleagues (25%). Meanwhile, globally, 10% of professionals said they would decline a role that was fully remote.

## Over 1 in 5 professionals in Japan concerned about skills relevance, but more than 50% plan to change careers or companies in 2021

With remote work having been an option for most professionals for over a year now, many of them have used this momentum in a positive way and decided to leverage their skills. Globally, professionals in Japan are the least confident about their current skill set, with more than 1 in 5 fearing that their current skills will not be relevant to the labour market in 5 years-time. In comparison, professionals in Africa are the most optimistic—58% responded that they are “very confident” about their current skill sets.

To stay employable in the future, 93% of respondents in Japan are willing to retrain or learn a new skill. For those who want to upskill but have not yet done so, the main reasons are the financial cost (43%), not having the assurance that this investment will result in higher compensation (17%), and no guarantee that this will strengthen job security or progression (33%).

Despite concerns about skills relevance, professionals in Japan have expressed intentions to switch professions in 2021 (23%) or stay in the same profession but change employers (29%). Less than one-third plan to stay in the same role with the same company.

# Robert Walters Japan announced the latest hiring trends for digital talent

Rapid growth in e-commerce and progress in DX accelerates demand for digital talent. Shortage of data security specialists leads to increased training efforts

Retail companies rush to recruit digital talent amidst rapid e-commerce growth Due to Covid-19, physical retail shops and restaurants have been heavily impacted by dwindling foot traffic and inbound tourism. On the other hand, more consumers are turning to e-commerce sites as well as online services as they spend an increasing amount of time at home. As changing consumer habits push more companies to drive omnichannel strategies with greater emphasis on the digital side, demand for digital talent within the retail industry is growing rapidly.

While hiring for most retail positions paused in 2020, e-commerce and digital related roles remained highly active. Nevertheless, the talent pool for English-speaking candidates with digital retail experience in Japan is extremely small since the domestic e-commerce market is still relatively new. The competition for talent is intensifying particularly for professionals with skills in digital marketing, strategic marketing, CRM, mobile advertising, search engine marketing, and analytics.

Traditionally, salaries offered in retail companies have not been as competitive as they have heavily relied on strong branding to secure talent. However, as demand for digital talent grows across multiple industries such as fintech, retail companies are no longer competing just among themselves. To attract professionals with digital skills, companies will need to prominently highlight career paths and attractive salaries as part of their employee value proposition.
